modules.title: Tour the data estate
modules.prerequisites: Facilitator setup complete
modules.question: What data do we have, how does it fit together, and which part do I want to work on today?
build: Nothing yet: you tour every data product in the account with Cortex Code, from corporate payments to retail customers and the branch network, then pick where to zoom in.

steps.title: Open Cortex Code
steps.body:
1. At the top left of Snowsight, switch the toggle from **Home** to **CoCo**.
2. Close the **CoCo mode (preview)** pop-up if it appears.
3. Press **New session**.
4. Paste each prompt in this module into the **How can I help?** box.
What's on the CoCo screen:
- **New session** starts a fresh chat. Start one for each module, so it begins with a clean context.
- **Automations** lists prompts scheduled to run on their own. You'll create one in GOV2.
When Cortex Code wants to run a query, it shows a **Run this command?** card:
- **Allow** lets it run
- **Skip** stops it
**Tip:** you're signed in as `HOL_PARTICIPANT`, with `BANKING_WH` and `BANKING_HOL` as your defaults. Cortex Code uses them, so you don't need to set a role or warehouse.
steps.where: Snowsight home page, the **Home / CoCo** toggle (top left) > **CoCo**
steps.expect: the Cortex Code screen with a **How can I help?** box
steps.mediaCaption: Home > CoCo, then paste the first prompt

steps.title: What data do we have?
steps.body: **Tip:** the **Data map** page of this app (top right) shows the same estate as a picture.
steps.prompt: Give me a tour of the BANKING_HOL database. For the RAW_DATA, RETAIL, ANALYTICS and AUDIT_PACK schemas, list every table with its row count and say whether it is Iceberg. Group them into data products: corporate payments, retail banking (the RB_ tables), branch network, analytics and governance.
steps.expect: about 33 tables and 1 view in five data products: nine corporate payments Iceberg tables (PAYMENTS has 50,000 rows), seven RB_ retail Iceberg tables (20,000 customers, about 1.3 million transactions), 57 branches with ATMs and drive times, and analytics and governance tables that fill in as you build

steps.title: How does it fit together?
steps.body: **Tip:** compare the diagram with the **Data map** page. The joins should match.
steps.prompt: How do these data products join? Draw a simple text diagram of the keys between them: corporate payments to accounts, customers and relationship managers, and retail customers to their home branch, products, employer and transactions. Point out any links that cross from one data product to another.
steps.expect: corporate PAYMENTS > ACCOUNTS > CUSTOMERS > RELATIONSHIP_MANAGERS; retail RB_CUSTOMERS > RB_ACCOUNTS > RB_PRODUCTS, plus RB_EMPLOYMENT and RB_TRANSACTIONS; and the bridge RB_CUSTOMERS.HOME_BRANCH_ID > RETAIL.BRANCHES, where retail customers meet the branch network

steps.title: Meet a retail customer
steps.body: **Tip:** the people are synthetic. The addresses, postcodes and area statistics are real open data.
steps.prompt: Pick one salaried retail customer from BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS who holds a mortgage. Show me their profile and area deprivation decile, their home branch and drive time from RETAIL.BRANCHES, their employer, gross and net monthly pay from RB_EMPLOYMENT, every product they hold by name from RB_ACCOUNTS joined to RB_PRODUCTS, their affordability band, and their last ten transactions.
steps.expect: one customer end to end: a real UK address, a home branch a few minutes' drive away, an employer and payroll credits on their pay day, products by name (such as a fixed mortgage and an easy access saver) and an affordability band

steps.title: Meet a corporate client
steps.prompt: Now do the same for one corporate client in BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS: their relationship manager, accounts, payment count and failure rate by payment scheme, and their most recent feedback.
steps.expect: one client, their RM, a few accounts, a failure rate by scheme (CHAPS, BACS, FPS and so on) and a feedback comment

steps.title: Pick your zoom
steps.body: Next: **C1** zooms into one data product, the corporate payments Iceberg tables. Every pathway starts there, then goes its own way.
steps.prompt: Based on what we've seen, suggest three questions a retail bank could answer with this data, one each for attrition, product affordability and fraud, and say which tables each would need.
steps.expect: three questions, each with the tables it would use

modules.check: Every data product is in your account, and you have queried the retail customer, product and employment tables.
modules.note: At a bank these would be separate data products with their own owners: payments operations, retail customer, branch network. Snowflake keeps them in one governed account, so a question that crosses them is a join, not a project.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- C0: TOUR THE DATA ESTATE - reference queries
-- What Cortex Code should arrive at for each C0 prompt. Run as HOL_PARTICIPANT.
-- =====================================================
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;

-- 1. What data do we have? Every table by data product, with row counts
SELECT CASE
         WHEN TABLE_SCHEMA = 'RAW_DATA' AND TABLE_NAME LIKE 'RB\\_%' THEN 'Retail banking'
         WHEN TABLE_SCHEMA = 'RAW_DATA' THEN 'Corporate payments'
         WHEN TABLE_SCHEMA = 'RETAIL' THEN 'Branch network'
         WHEN TABLE_SCHEMA = 'ANALYTICS' THEN 'Analytics'
         ELSE 'Governance' END AS DATA_PRODUCT,
       TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME, IS_ICEBERG, ROW_COUNT
FROM BANKING_HOL.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA IN ('RAW_DATA', 'RETAIL', 'ANALYTICS', 'AUDIT_PACK')
ORDER BY DATA_PRODUCT, TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME;

-- 2. How does it fit together? The retail bridge to the branch network
SELECT b.CITY, b.BRANCH_NAME, COUNT(*) AS RETAIL_CUSTOMERS, ROUND(AVG(c.HOME_BRANCH_DRIVE_S) / 60, 1) AS AVG_DRIVE_MIN
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.BRANCHES b ON b.BRANCH_ID = c.HOME_BRANCH_ID
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY RETAIL_CUSTOMERS DESC LIMIT 10;

-- 3. Meet a retail customer: profile, branch, employer and pay, products, affordability
WITH one AS (
    SELECT c.CUSTOMER_ID
    FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c
    JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_EMPLOYMENT e ON e.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
    JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_ACCOUNTS a ON a.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID AND a.PRODUCT = 'MORTGAGE'
    WHERE e.INCOME_SOURCE = 'SALARY' AND NOT c.CHURNED
    ORDER BY c.CUSTOMER_ID LIMIT 1
)
SELECT c.FIRST_NAME || ' ' || c.LAST_NAME AS CUSTOMER, c.AGE, c.ADDRESS_LINE_1, c.POSTCODE, c.CITY, c.IMD_DECILE,
       b.BRANCH_NAME AS HOME_BRANCH, ROUND(c.HOME_BRANCH_DRIVE_S / 60, 1) AS DRIVE_MIN,
       e.EMPLOYER_NAME, e.PAY_FREQUENCY, e.PAY_DAY, e.GROSS_ANNUAL_GBP, e.NET_MONTHLY_GBP,
       LISTAGG(p.PRODUCT_NAME, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY p.PRODUCT_FAMILY) AS PRODUCTS,
       c.TOTAL_DEBT_GBP, c.DISPOSABLE_INCOME_GBP, c.AFFORDABILITY_BAND
FROM one
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c ON c.CUSTOMER_ID = one.CUSTOMER_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.BRANCHES b ON b.BRANCH_ID = c.HOME_BRANCH_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_EMPLOYMENT e ON e.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_ACCOUNTS a ON a.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID AND a.STATUS = 'OPEN'
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_PRODUCTS p ON p.PRODUCT_ID = a.PRODUCT_ID
GROUP BY ALL;

-- 4. Meet a corporate client: RM, accounts, failure rate by scheme
SELECT cu.CUSTOMER_NAME, rm.RM_NAME, p.PAYMENT_TYPE, COUNT(*) AS PAYMENTS,
       ROUND(100 * COUNT_IF(p.STATUS = 'FAILED') / COUNT(*), 2) AS FAILED_PCT
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.PAYMENTS p
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.ACCOUNTS a ON a.ACCOUNT_ID = p.ORIGINATOR_ACCOUNT_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS cu ON cu.CUSTOMER_ID = a.CUSTOMER_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RELATIONSHIP_MANAGERS rm ON rm.RM_ID = cu.RM_ID
WHERE cu.CUSTOMER_ID = (SELECT MIN(CUSTOMER_ID) FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS)
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY PAYMENTS DESC;

modules.title: Explore the Iceberg data product
modules.prerequisites: C0
modules.question: What has the platform team published to us, and what can we (not) do with it?
build: Nothing yet: you zoom into one data product, the nine read-only corporate payments Iceberg tables, with Cortex Code, and get to know the Workspace you'll build everything else in.

steps.title: See what has been published
steps.where: the **CoCo** tab, in your C0 session or a **New session**
steps.prompt: List the corporate payments Iceberg tables in BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA (not the RB_ retail tables) with their row counts, and show the Iceberg metadata location for BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.PAYMENTS. Explain what Snowflake-managed Iceberg means for other engines reading this data.
steps.expect: nine Iceberg tables (PAYMENTS has 50,000 rows) and a metadata JSON location

steps.title: Go back Home and open the banking-hol-pack Workspace
steps.body:
1. Switch the toggle at the top left back to **Home**.
2. Click **Workspaces** (under Projects).
3. Open the **My Workspace** dropdown (top left) and pick **banking-hol-pack**.
What's in the Workspace:
- **+** creates SQL files, notebooks, dbt projects, Streamlit apps, agents, semantic views and pipelines
- the file explorer (left) holds the lab: `dbt/`, `notebooks/`, `vignettes/`
- the bottom panel has Query History and, later, the dbt pane
- Cortex Code is here too, as a sidebar: the round button at the bottom right
Use **banking-hol-pack** whenever a module says Workspace. Cortex Code only finds the lab files when it's open.
**Tip:** Snowsight sometimes reopens **My Workspace**. Check the name at the top left whenever you come back.
steps.where: the **Home / CoCo** toggle > **Home**, then **Projects > Workspaces** > the **My Workspace** dropdown (top left) > **banking-hol-pack**
steps.expect: the banking-hol-pack Workspace open, with `dbt/`, `notebooks/` and `vignettes/` in the file explorer
steps.mediaCaption: CoCo > Home > Workspaces > banking-hol-pack, then the Cortex Code sidebar

steps.title: Prove the guard-rails
steps.prompt: Try to insert a test row into BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.PAYMENTS using my current role, then explain the error and why the platform team set it up this way.
steps.expect: an "Insufficient privileges" error. That's intentional: sources are read-only.

steps.title: Learn the data model
steps.prompt: Describe the corporate payments tables in BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA (not the RB_ ones) and how they join together. Draw the relationships as a simple text diagram.
steps.expect: customers -> relationship managers, customers -> accounts -> payments (via ORIGINATOR_ACCOUNT_ID), plus feedback, alerts, schemes, SLAs and error codes

steps.title: Profile payments and build a first client 360
steps.prompt: Using BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA, show payment count, volume in GBP millions and success rate by PAYMENT_TYPE. Then list the 10 corporate clients with the most failed payments, with their RM, sector, account count and feedback count. Run both queries.
steps.expect: six payment schemes, then a top-10 client table ranked by failed payments, with each client's RM and sector

modules.check: Your role can read all nine corporate Iceberg tables but cannot insert into them.
modules.note: At a bank the same tables sit on the bank's own object storage via an external volume; the SQL is identical.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- BANKING HOL PACK - SHARED CORE
-- C1: EXPLORE THE PUBLISHED ICEBERG DATA PRODUCT  (~25 min, all personas)
--
-- Business context: you are part of Payments Operations for Corporate
-- Banking. The platform team has published nine source tables to the
-- enterprise data platform as Iceberg tables. You can read them but you
-- cannot load or change them - exactly like a bank's data platform.
-- =====================================================

USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;   -- see exactly what an attendee sees
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA;

-- C1.1 What has been published to us?
SHOW ICEBERG TABLES IN SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA;
-- Note the catalog (SNOWFLAKE) and that storage is Snowflake-managed.
-- At a bank the same tables sit on the bank's own object storage
-- via an external volume; the SQL you write is identical.

-- C1.2 Iceberg tables keep open metadata - this is what lets other engines
-- (Spark, Trino, etc.) read the same data with no copy.
SELECT SYSTEM$GET_ICEBERG_TABLE_INFORMATION('BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.PAYMENTS') AS ICEBERG_METADATA;

-- C1.3 Prove the guard-rails: attendees cannot load or modify source data.
-- Expect: "Insufficient privileges". This is intentional.
-- INSERT INTO PAYMENTS (PAYMENT_ID) VALUES ('TEST');

-- C1.4 Get to know the data model (see docs/data_sources.md for the ERD)
SELECT 'PAYMENTS' AS TABLE_NAME, COUNT(*) AS ROW_COUNT FROM PAYMENTS
UNION ALL SELECT 'CUSTOMER_FEEDBACK',     COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER_FEEDBACK
UNION ALL SELECT 'OPERATIONAL_ALERTS',    COUNT(*) FROM OPERATIONAL_ALERTS
UNION ALL SELECT 'CUSTOMERS',             COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMERS
UNION ALL SELECT 'ACCOUNTS',              COUNT(*) FROM ACCOUNTS
UNION ALL SELECT 'RELATIONSHIP_MANAGERS', COUNT(*) FROM RELATIONSHIP_MANAGERS
ORDER BY ROW_COUNT DESC;

-- C1.5 Payments mix by scheme - the six UK/international rails
SELECT PAYMENT_TYPE,
       COUNT(*)                                        AS PAYMENTS,
       ROUND(SUM(AMOUNT) / 1e6, 1)                     AS VOLUME_M,
       ROUND(COUNT_IF(STATUS = 'COMPLETED') / COUNT(*) * 100, 2) AS SUCCESS_RATE_PCT
FROM PAYMENTS
GROUP BY PAYMENT_TYPE
ORDER BY PAYMENTS DESC;

-- C1.6 A corporate client 360 in one query: customer -> RM -> accounts -> payments -> feedback
SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME, c.SECTOR, r.RM_NAME, r.TEAM,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.ACCOUNT_ID)                    AS ACCOUNTS,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.PAYMENT_ID)                    AS PAYMENTS,
       COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(p.STATUS = 'FAILED', p.PAYMENT_ID, NULL)) AS FAILED,
       COUNT(DISTINCT f.FEEDBACK_ID)                   AS FEEDBACK_ITEMS
FROM CUSTOMERS c
JOIN RELATIONSHIP_MANAGERS r ON c.RM_ID = r.RM_ID
JOIN ACCOUNTS a              ON a.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
LEFT JOIN PAYMENTS p         ON p.ORIGINATOR_ACCOUNT_ID = a.ACCOUNT_ID
LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER_FEEDBACK f ON f.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY FAILED DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- C1.7 Iceberg time travel works too: what did PAYMENTS look like an hour ago?
-- (Uncomment once the tables are at least a few minutes old.)
-- SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PAYMENTS AT (OFFSET => -60*5);

-- C1.8 Ask Cortex Code (CoCo panel in your Workspace):
--   "Describe the tables in BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA and how they join together."
--   "Which customers have the highest payment failure rate? Write the SQL and run it."

SELECT 'Core C1 complete - pick your pathway in pathways/' AS STATUS;

modules.title: Iceberg + dbt pipeline with Cortex Code
modules.prerequisites: Core C1 only
modules.question: Turn the published Iceberg sources into governed, tested data products - and publish them back to the lake as Iceberg.
build: The dbt project in the Workspace (4 staging views, 2 marts, pre-written tests), run from the Workspace dbt pane
Two Cortex Code-built marts: `mart_customer_payments`, `mart_rm_performance`
Nightly task `TSK_DBT_NIGHTLY_BUILD` (suspended)
Iceberg data product `DP_SLA_COMPLIANCE`

steps.title: Open the dbt project in the Workspace
steps.body:
1. Open `dbt/models/staging/schema.yml` in the file explorer.
2. Paste this prompt into the Cortex Code sidebar.
The sources in `schema.yml` point straight at the `RAW_DATA` Iceberg tables. dbt reads Iceberg exactly like native tables.
steps.where: Snowsight > **Projects > Workspaces** > **My Workspace** dropdown > **banking-hol-pack**, then `dbt/` in the file explorer
steps.prompt: Walk me through the dbt project in the dbt/ folder of this Workspace: what each staging and mart model does, where the sources come from, and which models are defined in models/marts/schema.yml but have no .sql file yet.
steps.expect: 4 staging models and 2 marts (`mart_payment_kpis`, `mart_sla_compliance`). `mart_customer_payments` and `mart_rm_performance` have tests in `schema.yml` but no SQL yet. Those are the two you'll build.
steps.mediaCaption: Home > Workspaces > banking-hol-pack, then the Cortex Code sidebar

steps.title: Run dbt build from the dbt pane
steps.body:
1. Open the **dbt** tab in the bottom panel. It shows Profile **dev** and a blue **Run** button.
2. Click the arrow next to **Run** to open **Select Operation**.
3. Choose **Build** and press **Execute**.
**Important:** choose **Build**, not **Run**. Run only creates the models and skips the tests that prove Cortex Code's marts are correct.
Build runs the models and their tests in dependency order.
steps.where: the bottom panel of the Workspace > **dbt** tab (next to Query History)
steps.expect: the Output tab ends with every model and test passing (`ERROR=0`). Open the **DAG** tab to see the lineage from the Iceberg sources to the marts.
steps.mediaCaption: Open a dbt file > bottom panel > dbt tab > arrow next to the blue button > Build

steps.title: Generate mart_customer_payments with Cortex Code
steps.where: the Cortex Code sidebar, with the banking-hol-pack Workspace open
steps.prompt: Create a dbt mart model dbt/models/marts/mart_customer_payments.sql that summarises payment activity per customer. Join stg_payments -> stg_accounts (on originator_account_id) -> stg_customers and follow the patterns in mart_payment_kpis.sql. Output one row per customer with these columns: customer_id, customer_name, customer_sector, rm_name, total_payments, total_volume_gbp, success_rate_pct (a float percentage, 0-100), avg_processing_time_ms and most_used_scheme. Keep the column names and tests already defined for this model in models/marts/schema.yml.
steps.expect: a new file `dbt/models/marts/mart_customer_payments.sql`. DE2 builds on this mart, so keep these column names.

steps.title: Generate mart_rm_performance with Cortex Code
steps.prompt: Create dbt/models/marts/mart_rm_performance.sql: one row per relationship manager with rm_id, rm_name, client_count, total_volume_gbp, avg_success_rate_pct and the name of their client with the lowest success rate. Build it from mart_customer_payments and stg_customers, and keep the column names and tests in models/marts/schema.yml. Then run dbt build for mart_rm_performance and its upstream models in this Workspace, and fix the model until every test passes.
steps.expect: a new file `dbt/models/marts/mart_rm_performance.sql`, and Cortex Code reporting the tests passing. If it only compiles the model, that's fine: the next step builds everything.

steps.title: Build the whole project and check the tests
steps.body:
1. Click the arrow next to **Run** to open **Select Operation**.
2. Choose **Build** and press **Execute**.
Writing or compiling a model doesn't create its table. Only a build does.
steps.where: the bottom panel of the Workspace > **dbt** tab
steps.expect: the Output shows 8 models and every test passing (`ERROR=0`), including the tests for both Cortex Code marts. If a test fails, paste the error into Cortex Code, ask it to fix the model, and Build again.
steps.mediaCaption: dbt tab > arrow next to the blue button > Build > Execute

steps.title: Deploy the project
steps.body:
The Workspace is where you develop. The deployed project object `BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.BANKING_DBT` is what production runs.
It was deployed when the lab was set up, so it doesn't have the marts you just wrote yet.
steps.prompt: Deploy the dbt project in my banking-hol-pack Workspace (snow://workspace/DEFAULT_DATABASE.PUBLIC."banking-hol-pack"/versions/live/dbt) to the existing dbt project object BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.BANKING_DBT with ALTER DBT PROJECT ... ADD VERSION FROM. Then list the models in the deployed project to confirm MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS and MART_RM_PERFORMANCE are included.
steps.expect: "Successfully deployed new files", and both Cortex Code marts listed in the deployed project. The nightly task in the next step now builds what you developed.

steps.title: Schedule the project
steps.body: **Autonomous Data Engineering:** native orchestration with a task, so the data product rebuilds itself every night with no external orchestrator.
steps.prompt: Create a task BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.TSK_DBT_NIGHTLY_BUILD on warehouse BANKING_WH that runs EXECUTE DBT PROJECT BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.BANKING_DBT ARGS = 'build' every day at 05:00 Europe/London. Leave it suspended.
steps.expect: the task created and suspended, on a 05:00 Europe/London schedule. In production you'd resume it. No external orchestrator needed.

steps.title: Publish the data product back to the lake as Iceberg
steps.prompt: Create a Snowflake-managed Iceberg table BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.DP_SLA_COMPLIANCE (CATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE') from MART_SLA_COMPLIANCE, casting PAYMENT_DAY to TIMESTAMP_NTZ(6) because Iceberg stores microseconds. Add a comment describing it as a data product, then show its Iceberg metadata location.
steps.expect: `DP_SLA_COMPLIANCE` listed by `SHOW ICEBERG TABLES IN SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS`, with a metadata location other engines can read

modules.check: `dbt build` in the dbt pane passes with `ERROR=0` once the two Cortex Code marts exist, and `DP_SLA_COMPLIANCE` is an Iceberg table in `ANALYTICS`.
modules.note: Production Iceberg tables use the bank's external volume (one volume, one IAM role across accounts) rather than Snowflake-managed storage. dbt models and SQL are otherwise identical.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- VIGNETTE DE1: ICEBERG + dbt PIPELINE WITH CORTEX CODE   (~60 min)
-- Persona: Data Engineer
-- Question: "Turn the published Iceberg sources into governed, tested
--            data products - and publish them back to the lake as Iceberg."
-- Prereq:   Core C1 only. (Produces everything core_analytics.sql would.)
--
-- Work in the lab Workspace banking-hol-pack (Projects > Workspaces > My Workspace dropdown), which is
-- already in your account. On your own account, create one from
-- https://github.com/sfc-gh-boconnor/banking_hol_pack (Projects > Workspaces >
-- From Git repository).
-- =====================================================

USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;   -- see exactly what an attendee sees
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE1.1 Walk the dbt project (Workspace file explorer: dbt/)
--   models/staging/schema.yml  - sources point at BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA (Iceberg)
--   models/staging/*.sql       - 4 views: cast, clean, denormalise
--   models/marts/*.sql         - mart_payment_kpis, mart_sla_compliance
--   macros/generate_schema_name.sql - land models in ANALYTICS, not ANALYTICS_ANALYTICS
-- dbt reads Iceberg sources exactly like native tables. No code changes.
-- -----------------------------------------------------

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE1.2 Deploy and run as a dbt Project on Snowflake
-- In the Workspace: open the dbt tab in the bottom panel, choose build from the
-- Run dropdown and run it.
-- Or from SQL / a task (this is how you would schedule it in production):
-- -----------------------------------------------------
EXECUTE DBT PROJECT BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.BANKING_DBT ARGS = 'build';
-- Expect: Done. PASS=27 WARN=0 ERROR=0

-- Schedule it - one task, no external orchestrator
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK TSK_DBT_NIGHTLY_BUILD
    WAREHOUSE = BANKING_WH
    SCHEDULE  = 'USING CRON 0 5 * * * Europe/London'
AS
    EXECUTE DBT PROJECT BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.BANKING_DBT ARGS = 'build';
-- Left suspended for the lab. In production: ALTER TASK TSK_DBT_NIGHTLY_BUILD RESUME;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE1.3 Accelerate with Cortex Code (CoCo panel in the Workspace)
-- Prompt 1:
--   "Create a dbt mart model mart_customer_payments in dbt/models/marts that
--    summarises payment activity per customer: total payments, total volume,
--    success rate and most-used payment scheme. Join stg_payments -> stg_accounts
--    -> stg_customers and follow the patterns in mart_payment_kpis.sql."
-- Prompt 2:
--   "Create mart_rm_performance: one row per relationship manager with rm_id,
--    rm_name, client_count, total volume, average success rate and their client
--    with the lowest success rate. Then run dbt build and fix any failing tests."
-- The tests for both models already exist in models/marts/schema.yml, so
-- `dbt build` proves CoCo's code is correct.
-- -----------------------------------------------------

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE1.4 Validate
-- -----------------------------------------------------
SELECT 'STG_PAYMENTS' AS OBJ, COUNT(*) AS ROWS_ FROM STG_PAYMENTS
UNION ALL SELECT 'MART_PAYMENT_KPIS',   COUNT(*) FROM MART_PAYMENT_KPIS
UNION ALL SELECT 'MART_SLA_COMPLIANCE', COUNT(*) FROM MART_SLA_COMPLIANCE;

SELECT SLA_STATUS, COUNT(*) AS SCHEME_DAYS
FROM MART_SLA_COMPLIANCE GROUP BY SLA_STATUS ORDER BY SCHEME_DAYS DESC;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE1.5 Publish the data product back to the lake as Iceberg
-- Consumers on other engines (Spark, Trino, etc.) can now read the mart with no copy.
-- Iceberg stores microsecond precision, so timestamps are cast to scale 6.
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE ICEBERG TABLE DP_SLA_COMPLIANCE
    CATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE'
    COMMENT = 'Data product: daily SLA compliance per payment scheme (Iceberg)'
AS SELECT * REPLACE (PAYMENT_DAY::TIMESTAMP_NTZ(6) AS PAYMENT_DAY)
   FROM MART_SLA_COMPLIANCE;

SELECT SYSTEM$GET_ICEBERG_TABLE_INFORMATION('BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.DP_SLA_COMPLIANCE') AS METADATA_LOCATION;

-- In your bank: in production the Iceberg table would use the bank's
-- EXTERNAL_VOLUME (one volume and one IAM role, shared across accounts)
-- instead of Snowflake-managed storage. The SQL above is otherwise unchanged.

SELECT 'DE1 complete' AS STATUS;

modules.title: Dynamic Tables + data quality

modules.question: Keep an ops-floor SLA monitor fresh without orchestration code, and prove the data feeding it is trustworthy.

steps.title: Orchestrate the pipeline with Pipeline Builder
steps.body:
1. In the **banking-hol-pack** Workspace, open the Workspace **Home** tab (the house icon at the top of the file explorer). This is the Home tab inside Workspaces, not the main Snowsight Home.
2. Press the **Pipeline Builder** icon.
3. In the **Create Pipeline Builder** dialog, set:
- name: `payments_nightly`
- **Database and schema**: **BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS**
4. Click **Generate with Cortex** at the bottom left of the dialog.
5. In the **Prompt** box that opens, paste this prompt and click **Generate**.
**Important:** don't pick `RAW_DATA`. The Iceberg sources are read-only, so creating it there fails with "must have CREATE DCM PROJECT".
**Tip:** click **Generate with Cortex**, not **Create**. Create opens an empty canvas.
Dynamic tables keep themselves fresh, but the dbt build and the data quality checks need scheduling. Pipeline Builder draws that as a task graph.
**Autonomous Data Engineering:** describe a pipeline in plain English, refine it visually, and deploy it as a native **task graph** (public preview). No external orchestrator needed.
steps.prompt: Build a nightly pipeline in BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS on warehouse BANKING_WH, scheduled at 05:00 Europe/London. Task 1 BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.PIPE_DBT_BUILD runs EXECUTE DBT PROJECT BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.BANKING_DBT ARGS = 'build'. Task 2 BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.PIPE_REFRESH_SLA runs after it: ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.DT_LIVE_SLA_BREACHES REFRESH. Task 3 BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.PIPE_DQ_CHECKS runs after task 1: SELECT the NULL_COUNT on RM_NAME and DUPLICATE_COUNT on CUSTOMER_ID of BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS. Set warehouse BANKING_WH on each of the three tasks itself, not as a task-graph default. Set the task graph's desired state to Suspended so nothing runs after deploy.
steps.expect: Cortex first drafts a plan (the three tasks, their order, the 05:00 schedule and the warehouse) and asks you to **Proceed**, **Modify** or **Cancel**. Check the plan matches the prompt and choose **Proceed** (or **Modify** to correct it). You then get a canvas with three connected tasks (dbt build, then the dynamic table refresh and the data quality checks). Before you deploy, open the task graph's settings (**Objects > Task graphs**, or select a task > **Graph** tab > **Edit graph settings**) and check **Desired state** is **Suspended**: Generate with Cortex can set it to Resumed, and the canvas Deploy uses whatever the project files say. Then **Deploy**, review the planned changes and **Deploy** again. Once it's created, refresh the file explorer if needed and open `payments_nightly` from the sidebar. Click any step on the canvas to see its details, and use **Deploy** to run the pipeline or create a task from it. To view the pipeline later, open it from its `payments_nightly` link in the Workspace (or hover over the folder in the file explorer and select the **Open pipeline builder** icon); after the first deploy, **Deployed Project** on the canvas toolbar opens it in Snowsight, where the task graph's **Graph** tab shows the run order. The tasks and the task graph are created suspended in `ANALYTICS`, and you can see them under **Monitoring > Task History**. Pipeline Builder orchestrates tasks; it doesn't create the dynamic tables themselves, which is why you built those first. If you build the pipeline a second time and **Deploy** fails with "cannot change orchestration model while ... PIPE_DBT_BUILD is not suspended", tasks from your first attempt are still running: ask Cortex Code to suspend `BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.PIPE_DBT_BUILD`, then deploy again.

modules.note: Real-time payments streaming is out of scope at many banks today; dynamic tables give near-real-time freshness over data the platform already lands.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- VIGNETTE DE2: DYNAMIC TABLES + DATA QUALITY   (~45 min)
-- Persona: Data Engineer
-- Question: "How do I keep an ops-floor SLA monitor fresh without writing
--            orchestration, and prove the data feeding it is trustworthy?"
-- Prereq:   setup/catchup/core_analytics.sql  (or DE1 + DA1)
-- =====================================================

USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;   -- see exactly what an attendee sees
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE2.1 Dynamic Tables: declare the result, Snowflake keeps it fresh
-- -----------------------------------------------------

-- Ops-floor SLA breach monitor: never more than 1 minute stale
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE DT_LIVE_SLA_BREACHES
    TARGET_LAG = '1 minute'
    WAREHOUSE  = BANKING_WH
AS
SELECT PAYMENT_TYPE,
       SUM(TOTAL_PAYMENTS)  AS TOTAL_PAYMENTS,
       SUM(FAILED_PAYMENTS) AS BREACHED_PAYMENTS,
       ROUND(SUM(FAILED_PAYMENTS)::FLOAT / NULLIF(SUM(TOTAL_PAYMENTS), 0) * 100, 2) AS BREACH_RATE_PCT,
       MIN(PAYMENT_DAY) AS EARLIEST_BREACH,
       MAX(PAYMENT_DAY) AS LATEST_BREACH
FROM MART_SLA_COMPLIANCE
WHERE SLA_STATUS = 'BREACH'
GROUP BY PAYMENT_TYPE;

-- Failed-payment triage feed built straight off the Iceberg source.
-- Dynamic tables can read Iceberg tables directly - no copy into Snowflake storage.
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE DT_FAILED_PAYMENT_TRIAGE
    TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM
    WAREHOUSE  = BANKING_WH
AS
SELECT p.PAYMENT_ID, p.PAYMENT_DATE, p.PAYMENT_TYPE, p.AMOUNT, p.CURRENCY,
       p.ERROR_CODE, e.ERROR_DESCRIPTION, e.ERROR_CATEGORY, e.IS_RETRYABLE,
       c.CUSTOMER_NAME, c.SECTOR, r.RM_NAME
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.PAYMENTS p
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.ERROR_CODES e  ON p.ERROR_CODE = e.ERROR_CODE
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.ACCOUNTS a     ON p.ORIGINATOR_ACCOUNT_ID = a.ACCOUNT_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS c    ON a.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RELATIONSHIP_MANAGERS r ON c.RM_ID = r.RM_ID
WHERE p.STATUS IN ('FAILED', 'RETURNED');

-- Downstream summary chained off the triage feed
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE DT_RETRYABLE_SUMMARY
    TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'
    WAREHOUSE  = BANKING_WH
AS
SELECT PAYMENT_TYPE, ERROR_CATEGORY, IS_RETRYABLE,
       COUNT(*) AS PAYMENTS, ROUND(SUM(AMOUNT), 2) AS VALUE_AT_RISK
FROM DT_FAILED_PAYMENT_TRIAGE
GROUP BY ALL;

SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES IN SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS;

-- Refresh history and the pipeline graph are also visible in Snowsight:
-- Monitoring > Dynamic Tables > DT_RETRYABLE_SUMMARY > Graph
SELECT NAME, STATE, REFRESH_ACTION, REFRESH_TRIGGER, DATA_TIMESTAMP
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.DYNAMIC_TABLE_REFRESH_HISTORY())
WHERE NAME LIKE 'DT_%'
ORDER BY DATA_TIMESTAMP DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE2.2 Data Metric Functions: quality checks that run on a schedule
-- -----------------------------------------------------

-- Schedule is set per table; changes also trigger a check
ALTER TABLE MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS SET DATA_METRIC_SCHEDULE = 'TRIGGER_ON_CHANGES';

-- System DMFs
ALTER TABLE MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS ADD DATA METRIC FUNCTION
    SNOWFLAKE.CORE.NULL_COUNT ON (RM_NAME);
ALTER TABLE MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS ADD DATA METRIC FUNCTION
    SNOWFLAKE.CORE.DUPLICATE_COUNT ON (CUSTOMER_ID);

-- A custom, business-rule DMF: success rate must be a valid percentage
-- (the argument type must match the column type - SUCCESS_RATE_PCT is FLOAT)
CREATE OR REPLACE DATA METRIC FUNCTION INVALID_SUCCESS_RATE_COUNT(
    t TABLE (SUCCESS_RATE_PCT FLOAT))
RETURNS NUMBER
AS
$$
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
    WHERE SUCCESS_RATE_PCT IS NULL OR SUCCESS_RATE_PCT < 0 OR SUCCESS_RATE_PCT > 100
$$;

ALTER TABLE MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS ADD DATA METRIC FUNCTION
    INVALID_SUCCESS_RATE_COUNT ON (SUCCESS_RATE_PCT);

-- Expectations: turn a metric into a pass/fail rule
ALTER TABLE MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS MODIFY DATA METRIC FUNCTION
    SNOWFLAKE.CORE.DUPLICATE_COUNT ON (CUSTOMER_ID)
    ADD EXPECTATION NO_DUPLICATE_CUSTOMERS (VALUE = 0);

-- Which checks are attached?
SELECT METRIC_NAME, REF_ARGUMENTS, SCHEDULE, SCHEDULE_STATUS
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.DATA_METRIC_FUNCTION_REFERENCES(
    REF_ENTITY_NAME   => 'BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS',
    REF_ENTITY_DOMAIN => 'TABLE'));

-- Run the checks on demand (scheduled results land in
-- SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.DATA_QUALITY_MONITORING_RESULTS after a few minutes)
SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORE.NULL_COUNT(SELECT RM_NAME FROM MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS)        AS NULL_RM_NAMES,
       SNOWFLAKE.CORE.DUPLICATE_COUNT(SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS) AS DUPLICATE_CUSTOMERS,
       INVALID_SUCCESS_RATE_COUNT(SELECT SUCCESS_RATE_PCT FROM MART_CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS) AS INVALID_RATES;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE2.3 Cortex Code prompts (try in the CoCo panel)
-- -----------------------------------------------------
--  "Add a dynamic table DT_HIGH_VALUE_FAILURES in BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS showing
--   failed CHAPS payments over 1m GBP with the customer and RM, refreshing every
--   2 minutes. Then show me its refresh history."
--  "Add a data metric function to MART_PAYMENT_KPIS that counts rows where
--   P95_PROCESSING_TIME_MS is less than AVG_PROCESSING_TIME_MS, and attach it."

SELECT 'DE2 complete' AS STATUS;

modules.title: Real-time payments: stream, mirror, serve, act
modules.prerequisites: C1 only. Uses `BANKING_HOL.REALTIME`, the shared interactive warehouse `HOL_INTERACTIVE_WH`, and grants to create a Snowflake Postgres instance and mirror it (all set up at provisioning)
modules.question: A corporate client's payments are failing right now. How does the operations floor see it within seconds, not after tonight's dbt build, and serve that view to everyone watching at once?
build: A **Snowflake Postgres** instance `HOL_PAYMENTS_PG`: the operational payments database the payment engine writes to
A live feed of payment events into Postgres, with an incident hidden in the stream
A **Data Mirror** that streams every change from Postgres into **Snowflake-managed Iceberg** tables in `PAYMENTS_MIRROR`, with `$live` (seconds behind) and `$changes` (the change feed)
Ops-floor queries served from the **interactive warehouse** `HOL_INTERACTIVE_WH`, straight off the mirrored table
Dynamic table `DT_PAYMENT_INCIDENTS` that flags failing payment clusters within a minute

steps.title: Open the starter notebook and create its service
steps.body:
1. Open `notebooks/` > **de3_realtime_payments.ipynb** in the file explorer.
- Can't see `notebooks/` and `vignettes/`? You're in the wrong Workspace. Pick **banking-hol-pack** from the Workspace dropdown (top left).
2. In the notebook toolbar, click the arrow next to the status dot (right of the blue run button).
3. Choose **Create new service**.
- Already created one in another module? Pick it under **Select service** instead, usually `USER_SERVICE_1`.
4. Expand **Service settings** in **Connect your notebook** and fill it in as below. Only the three **bold** rows change.
| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Service name | leave the default (e.g. `USER_SERVICE_1`) |
| Artifact repositories | leave as is (`SNOWFLAKE.SNOWPARK.PYPI_SHARED_REPOSITORY`) |
| Enable distributed compute | off |
| Runtime | leave as is (v3.0 · Python 3.12) |
| Compute type | CPU |
| Custom image | leave empty |
| **Compute pool** | **NOTEBOOK_POOL** (change it from HOL_COMPUTE_POOL_CPU) |
| **Idle timeout** | **1 hour** (change it from 24 hours) |
| **External access integrations** | **HOL_NOTEBOOK_ACCESS_INTEGRATION** (lets notebooks reach Postgres and the AI Gateway; set it here so one service works for every notebook module) |
| Secrets | leave empty |
5. Click **Create and connect**. The first start takes 1-2 minutes.
6. Check the role is **HOL_PARTICIPANT** and the warehouse is **BANKING_WH** (role and warehouse button in the notebook toolbar).
The starter notebook has one numbered heading per step, so Cortex Code puts each cell in the right place.
A notebook runs on its own **notebook service**, which you create once.
steps.where: the **banking-hol-pack** Workspace (not My Workspace) > file explorer > `notebooks/de3_realtime_payments.ipynb`
steps.expect: the starter notebook open in banking-hol-pack with its numbered headings, and the status dot showing the service connected
steps.mediaCaption: Open the notebook > Create new service > NOTEBOOK_POOL, 1 hour, HOL_NOTEBOOK_ACCESS_INTEGRATION

steps.title: Create the Postgres instance
steps.body: You don't write the Postgres code yourself. The cells import a tested helper in the Workspace, `vignettes/de3_realtime_payments/de3_postgres.py`.
steps.where: the Cortex Code sidebar, with `de3_realtime_payments` open
steps.prompt: In the open notebook de3_realtime_payments, put each cell I ask for under its matching numbered heading. Under heading 1, add a Python cell named create_pg that runs !pip install psycopg2-binary, makes vignettes/de3_realtime_payments/de3_postgres.py importable (search upwards from the current working directory for a folder containing vignettes/de3_realtime_payments/de3_postgres.py and add that folder to sys.path), imports de3_postgres as pg, and runs host = pg.create_postgres(get_active_session()). Don't rewrite the helper and never print the password. Then add a markdown cell explaining what create_postgres does: the instance size and why, the network policy, and what happens to the one-time password.
steps.expect: the cell prints the instance moving through CREATING, STARTING and FINALIZING, then returns its host after 3 to 5 minutes. `HOL_PAYMENTS_PG` uses `STANDARD_M`, the smallest size Data Mirroring supports, with the network policy `HOL_PG_POLICY`. Its `snowflake_admin` password is shown only once, in the CREATE result, so the helper saves it straight into the secret `BANKING_HOL.REALTIME.PG_ADMIN_SECRET` without printing it.

steps.title: Reveal the connection and connect
steps.body:
1. In the Lab Companion, click **Reveal Postgres connection**. It shows the host, user and password with copy buttons.
2. In the notebook, find the connection cell under heading 2 (`PG_HOST`, `PG_USER`, `PG_PASS`).
3. Replace each `<...>` placeholder with the value you copied, keeping the quotes.
4. Run the cell.
5. Paste this prompt into the Cortex Code sidebar:
steps.where: the Lab Companion > **DE3** > **Reveal Postgres connection**, then the notebook
steps.prompt: Under heading 2, after my connection cell, add a Python cell named source_table that opens conn = pg.connect(PG_HOST, PG_USER, PG_PASS) and runs pg.create_source_table(conn), printing the row count it returns. Then explain the table it created in Postgres and why it has a primary key.
steps.expect: `0` rows in the new Postgres table `payments.payment_events`. The primary key lets the mirror carry updates and deletes as well as inserts. Keep the password out of anything you share. You can reveal it again any time, for example after a kernel restart. If the Lab Companion says the password wasn't saved, run `pg.reset_password(get_active_session())` and reveal again. The instance only accepts connections from Snowflake (its network policy allows Snowflake's egress IP ranges), so connect from the notebook: a desktop client such as psql or DBeaver on your laptop will time out.

steps.title: Mirror Postgres into Snowflake
steps.prompt: Under heading 3, add a Python cell named mirror that runs pg.start_mirror(get_active_session()) and shows the result as a table. Then add a markdown cell explaining Snowflake Postgres Data Mirroring: what CREATE_MIRROR creates in PAYMENTS_MIRROR (an Iceberg table plus $live and $changes), who owns it, and what refresh_interval means.
steps.expect: `payments.payment_events` in state `REPLICATING` in the new database `PAYMENTS_MIRROR`. The mirror owns `PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS`, a Snowflake-managed Iceberg table in open Parquet, plus `PAYMENT_EVENTS$live` (the table plus changes not merged yet, so it's seconds behind) and `PAYMENT_EVENTS$changes` (the change feed). Changes merge into the base table every minute (`refresh_interval`). Nothing to schedule or run: the mirror keeps going on its own.

steps.title: Stream payments into Postgres
steps.prompt: Under heading 4, add a Python cell named stream that runs pg.stream_payments(conn, get_active_session()) to insert about 20 payment events a second into Postgres for 5 minutes, and prints the total it returns. Then explain in a markdown cell what the stream sends, including the SEPA incident in the second half.
steps.expect: the cell runs for 5 minutes, printing progress every 30 seconds, and sends about 6,000 events. While it runs, open a SQL worksheet and run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS$live` a few times: the count climbs about 20 to 40 seconds behind Postgres. Halfway through, one corporate client's SEPA payments start failing with "Beneficiary bank unavailable". The stream cell itself only prints how many events it sent (it doesn't report failures): you'll see the failed payments in the freshness check in the next step, spread through the run.

steps.title: Measure how fresh the data is
steps.prompt: Under heading 5, add a SQL cell named freshness: events and failed events per minute for the last 15 minutes from PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS$live, then the seconds between the newest EVENT_TS and SYSDATE() in both PAYMENT_EVENTS$live and the base table PAYMENT_EVENTS, then the count of rows per _CHANGE_TYPE in PAYMENT_EVENTS$changes. Run it and explain what the numbers say about end-to-end latency from Postgres to Snowflake.
steps.expect: about 1,200 events a minute while streaming, with `$live` about 20 to 40 seconds behind and the base table up to a minute behind (its refresh interval). Failures jump in the second half: that's the incident. `$changes` shows one `I` (insert) per event; an update would appear as a `D` and an `I`.

steps.title: Serve the ops floor from the interactive warehouse
steps.prompt: Under heading 6, add a SQL cell named ops_floor that runs USE WAREHOUSE HOL_INTERACTIVE_WH, then the queries a payments operations dashboard would refresh every few seconds directly on PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS: failed payments and failed value by scheme in the last 15 minutes, and the 10 clients with the most failed value in the last 15 minutes joined to BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS for the name. Then switch back with USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH. Run it and explain zero-copy interactive analytics on an Iceberg table: why there's no copy or conversion, and when the 5 second statement limit matters.
steps.expect: answers from `HOL_INTERACTIVE_WH` in well under a second once it's warm, straight off the mirrored Iceberg table, with no copy. SEPA stands out, and one client has a cluster of failed SEPA payments. On a few thousand rows a standard warehouse is quick too: the interactive warehouse earns its keep when hundreds of screens, APIs or agents run these queries every few seconds at once. Heavy one-off analysis belongs on a standard warehouse, and DML is rejected, which is why the cell switches back.

steps.title: Flag incidents automatically
steps.prompt: Under heading 7, add a SQL cell named incidents that creates the dynamic table BANKING_HOL.REALTIME.DT_PAYMENT_INCIDENTS with TARGET_LAG '1 minute' on warehouse BANKING_WH: failed payments in PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS from the last 15 minutes grouped by CUSTOMER_ID (with CUSTOMER_NAME from BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS), SCHEME and FAILURE_REASON, with the failed count, failed value, first and last failure, keeping groups with at least 5 failures. Then query it, largest first, then add a Python cell named draft_message that takes the top incident's real values (client, RM, scheme, failure reason, failed count and value, first and last failure) and fills them into a message template to the client's relationship manager, rendered with st.markdown or display(Markdown(...)) so the actual numbers appear.
steps.expect: one incident: Crown Logistics' SEPA payments failing with "Beneficiary bank unavailable", with the count, value and time window. The table refreshes every minute on its own, so the moment a new cluster starts in Postgres, it appears here. This is the same pattern as DE2's live SLA breaches, now on data streaming out of an operational database. Cortex Code automations (GOV2) could post it to the ops team.

modules.check: `HOL_PAYMENTS_PG` is READY, `PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS` is replicating with at least 1,000 events, and `DT_PAYMENT_INCIDENTS` exists.
modules.note: One platform takes payments from the operational database to an answer in seconds: written to Snowflake Postgres, mirrored continuously into open Iceberg tables, flagged by a dynamic table, and served to every screen on the ops floor by an interactive warehouse, with the same governance as the rest of the data.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- DE3: Real-time payments - reference SQL
-- The Postgres side is Python (de3_postgres.py); this is the Snowflake SQL around it.
-- Flow: Snowflake Postgres HOL_PAYMENTS_PG -> Data Mirror -> Snowflake-managed Iceberg
--       PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS (+ $live, $changes) -> interactive warehouse, dynamic table
-- =====================================================
USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;

-- 1. The instance (create_postgres runs the CREATE and saves the one-time password in the secret):
--    CREATE POSTGRES INSTANCE HOL_PAYMENTS_PG COMPUTE_FAMILY = 'STANDARD_M' STORAGE_SIZE_GB = 10
--      AUTHENTICATION_AUTHORITY = POSTGRES POSTGRES_VERSION = 18 NETWORK_POLICY = 'HOL_PG_POLICY';
SHOW POSTGRES INSTANCES LIKE 'HOL_PAYMENTS_PG';
DESCRIBE SECRET BANKING_HOL.REALTIME.PG_ADMIN_SECRET;   -- metadata only: the password isn't shown

-- 2. The mirror (start_mirror runs these)
GRANT USAGE ON POSTGRES INSTANCE HOL_PAYMENTS_PG TO APPLICATION SNOWFLAKE;
-- CALL SNOWFLAKE.POSTGRES.CREATE_MIRROR(
--     mirror_name => 'payments_mirror', postgres_instance => 'HOL_PAYMENTS_PG', postgres_database => 'postgres',
--     target_database => 'PAYMENTS_MIRROR', postgres_schemas => ['payments'],
--     refresh_interval => '1 minute', target_table_type => 'ICEBERG');
SELECT * FROM TABLE(SNOWFLAKE.POSTGRES.LIST_MIRRORS());
CALL SNOWFLAKE.POSTGRES.LIST_MIRRORED_TABLES('payments_mirror');
SHOW TABLES IN DATABASE PAYMENTS_MIRROR;   -- PAYMENT_EVENTS (Iceberg) and PAYMENT_EVENTS$CHANGES, owned by the mirror

-- 3. Freshness: volume and failures per minute, and how far each view is behind
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('minute', EVENT_TS) AS MINUTE, COUNT(*) AS EVENTS, COUNT_IF(STATUS = 'FAILED') AS FAILED
FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS$live
WHERE EVENT_TS >= DATEADD('minute', -15, SYSDATE())
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

SELECT 'live' AS VIEW_NAME, DATEDIFF('second', MAX(EVENT_TS), SYSDATE()) AS SECONDS_BEHIND FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS$live
UNION ALL
SELECT 'base Iceberg table', DATEDIFF('second', MAX(EVENT_TS), SYSDATE()) FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS;

-- The change feed: I = insert, D = delete (an update is a D plus an I)
SELECT _CHANGE_TYPE, COUNT(*) AS CHANGES FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS$changes GROUP BY 1;

-- 4. Ops floor on the shared interactive warehouse: zero-copy, straight off the mirrored Iceberg table
USE WAREHOUSE HOL_INTERACTIVE_WH;

SELECT SCHEME, COUNT(*) AS FAILED_PAYMENTS, SUM(AMOUNT) AS FAILED_VALUE
FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS
WHERE STATUS = 'FAILED' AND EVENT_TS >= DATEADD('minute', -15, SYSDATE())
GROUP BY SCHEME
ORDER BY FAILED_VALUE DESC;

SELECT c.CUSTOMER_NAME, e.SCHEME, COUNT(*) AS FAILED_PAYMENTS, SUM(e.AMOUNT) AS FAILED_VALUE
FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS e
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS c ON c.CUSTOMER_ID = e.CUSTOMER_ID
WHERE e.STATUS = 'FAILED' AND e.EVENT_TS >= DATEADD('minute', -15, SYSDATE())
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY FAILED_VALUE DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Interactive warehouses reject DML and procedures: switch back before creating anything
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;

-- 5. Incidents: failing clusters in the last 15 minutes, refreshed every minute
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE BANKING_HOL.REALTIME.DT_PAYMENT_INCIDENTS
  TARGET_LAG = '1 minute'
  WAREHOUSE = BANKING_WH
  COMMENT = 'DE3: failing payment clusters in the last 15 minutes, refreshed every minute'
AS
SELECT e.CUSTOMER_ID,
       c.CUSTOMER_NAME,
       e.SCHEME,
       e.FAILURE_REASON,
       COUNT(*)         AS FAILED_PAYMENTS,
       SUM(e.AMOUNT)    AS FAILED_VALUE,
       MIN(e.EVENT_TS)  AS FIRST_FAILURE,
       MAX(e.EVENT_TS)  AS LAST_FAILURE
FROM PAYMENTS_MIRROR.PAYMENTS.PAYMENT_EVENTS e
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.CUSTOMERS c ON c.CUSTOMER_ID = e.CUSTOMER_ID
WHERE e.STATUS = 'FAILED'
  AND e.EVENT_TS >= DATEADD('minute', -15, SYSDATE())
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

SELECT * FROM BANKING_HOL.REALTIME.DT_PAYMENT_INCIDENTS ORDER BY FAILED_PAYMENTS DESC;

-- 6. After the lab: the instance bills while it runs
-- ALTER POSTGRES INSTANCE HOL_PAYMENTS_PG SUSPEND;
-- Facilitator teardown: CALL SNOWFLAKE.POSTGRES.DROP_MIRROR(mirror_name => 'payments_mirror', drop_target_database => TRUE);
--                       DROP POSTGRES INSTANCE HOL_PAYMENTS_PG;

modules.title: Spark on Snowflake: run your PySpark and monitor it
modules.prerequisites: C1 only. Uses the raw status feed `BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB.PAYMENT_STATUS_UPDATES` and the Iceberg payments, both built at provisioning
modules.question: Our nightly payments pipelines are PySpark jobs on clusters we size, patch and pay for when they're idle. Can we run the same Spark code on Snowflake, against the same governed data, and see every run, failure and slow step in one place?
build: An interactive **Spark session** in a Workspace notebook, named so it shows up in **Monitoring > Spark > Spark Sessions**

A starter notebook with the PySpark already in it, and a bronze to silver to gold pipeline: quarantine bad rows, change data capture (duplicates and late arrivals handled), apply the latest status over the Iceberg payments, reconcile, and summarise failed payments for operations
Tables `PAYMENT_UPDATES_QUARANTINE`, `PAYMENTS_CURRENT`, `PIPELINE_RECONCILIATION` and `FAILED_PAYMENTS_BY_SCHEME` in `BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB`
The same pipeline as a **batch job** with `EXECUTE CODE BUNDLE`, straight from the lab's git repo, scheduled nightly by a task
A deliberately failed run, found and diagnosed in **Monitoring > Spark**, and an alert `SPARK_JOB_FAILURE_ALERT` that records every failed Spark job

steps.title: Open the starter notebook
steps.body:
1. Open `notebooks/` > **de4_spark_on_snowflake.ipynb**. The PySpark is already in it: one numbered heading per step, the cells underneath, and the prompt to paste above them.
2. Connect it to your notebook service (the arrow next to the status dot > **Select service**). No service yet? Create one as in DE3's first step: compute pool **NOTEBOOK_POOL**, idle timeout **1 hour**.
3. Under heading 0, run the **install** cell. It installs `snowpark-connect` (PySpark plus a Java runtime) from the Snowflake PyPI repository on your notebook service. If it says **Installed**, restart the kernel (Connect > **Restart kernel**).
4. Run the **context** cell. It sets the role, warehouse, database and schema: Snowpark Connect needs them before the session starts.
5. Open Snowsight > **Monitoring > Spark** in a second browser tab and keep it open.
steps.expect: your user, `HOL_PARTICIPANT`, `BANKING_HOL` and `SPARK_LAB` printed. The install takes a minute or two the first time; the service keeps it until it's recreated.
steps.mediaCaption: Open de4_spark_on_snowflake > service dropdown > NOTEBOOK_POOL, 1 hour

steps.title: Start a Spark session
steps.where: the Cortex Code sidebar, with `de4_spark_on_snowflake` open
steps.prompt: Explain the spark_session cell in de4_spark_on_snowflake: what Snowpark Connect for Spark is, what runs where when I call a DataFrame action, and where the app name appears in Snowsight. Then run it.
steps.expect: a Spark version and your session name, `de4_<your user>`, printed in a few seconds. Spark Monitoring in the Snowsight UI comes in the last step; if you opened it earlier, the session is listed there by that name with you as the owner.

steps.title: Explore the feed with PySpark
steps.prompt: Run the explore cell in de4_spark_on_snowflake and explain each number: what would break downstream if we loaded this feed as it is, ordered by LOADED_AT? Then open my session in Monitoring > Spark and tell me what I'll find there.
steps.expect: about 10,800 events but about 500 fewer distinct ones (duplicate deliveries), 40 rows with no payment id or an unknown status, about 20 payments the bank doesn't hold, and several hundred payments whose PROCESSING event arrived after their final status. Exact counts vary a little by account, because the payments are generated when the lab is installed. Load by `LOADED_AT` and those payments would go back to PROCESSING. In **Monitoring > Spark**, open your session: every DataFrame action is listed as a Snowflake query, each linked to its Query Profile.

steps.title: Build the pipeline
steps.prompt: Run the pipeline cell in de4_spark_on_snowflake, then walk me through it step by step: the quarantine rules, how the row_number window handles duplicates and late arrivals, and what the reconciliation proves.
steps.expect: 60 rows quarantined, 20 for each reason, `PAYMENTS_CURRENT` with 50,000 rows (the same as the source) and about 5,200 payments updated by the feed: both reconciliation lines `True`.

steps.title: Run it as a nightly batch job
steps.prompt: Run the batch_job, reconciliation and gold cells in de4_spark_on_snowflake and explain what EXECUTE CODE BUNDLE did. Then tell me what to look at for the payments_nightly run in Monitoring > Spark > Batch Jobs, including the Trace tab.
steps.expect: the **batch_job** cell takes about 30 to 60 seconds on the warehouse, with no cluster to start. Both reconciliation checks pass, and the gold table shows failed and returned payments by scheme. In **Monitoring > Spark > Batch Jobs**, open `payments_nightly`: the command, its queries, its logs and the **Trace** tab, one span per DataFrame action.
steps.mediaCaption: (what Monitoring shows after this step) Monitoring > Spark > Batch Jobs > payments_nightly > Telemetry (one span per DataFrame action)

steps.title: Schedule it
steps.prompt: Run the schedule cell in de4_spark_on_snowflake and explain the task: when it runs, what it runs, and how I'd chain it after the dbt build from DE1.
steps.expect: the task created and resumed, to run at 02:00 London time. The scheduler is Snowflake itself: no Airflow or cluster scheduler to run.

steps.title: Break it and find out why
steps.body: Then: don't fix the cell. The fix is the **batch_job** cell from step 4, which already reads the real feed. Leave the failed run in place, because the alert in the next step has to find it, and go on to heading 7.
steps.prompt: The broken_run cell in de4_spark_on_snowflake failed. Find out why from Snowflake: query SNOWFLAKE.SNOWPARK_CONNECT.GET_SPARK_APPLICATION_HISTORY for my latest failed run, then its ERROR logs in SNOWFLAKE.TELEMETRY.EVENTS_VIEW (filter RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES['snow.query.id'] on the run's EXECUTE_QUERY_ID), and tell me the root cause and the fix.
steps.expect: the **broken_run** cell fails in about 20 seconds, as intended: upstream "renamed" the feed. In **Monitoring > Spark > Batch Jobs**, `payments_nightly_broken` is **FAILED**, and its **Logs** show `AnalysisException: [TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND] ... PAYMENT_STATUS_UPDATES_V2` with the stack trace (logs can take a minute or two to arrive). Cortex Code finds the same from SQL and names the fix: drop `--source` or point it at `PAYMENT_STATUS_UPDATES`.
steps.mediaCaption: (what Monitoring shows after this step) Monitoring > Spark > Batch Jobs > payments_nightly_broken (Failed) > Telemetry

steps.title: Alert on failed Spark jobs
steps.prompt: Run the cells under heading 7 (spark_history through failures) in de4_spark_on_snowflake and explain how the alert finds each failure exactly once. How would I change the action to email the on-call engineer?
steps.expect: your sessions and batch runs as a table, the same data as **Monitoring > Spark**, then `payments_nightly_broken` in `SPARK_JOB_FAILURES` about a minute after **alert_now**. In production the action would email the on-call engineer or open a ticket; here it records the failure so nothing leaves the lab.

steps.title: See it all in Spark Monitoring
steps.body:
You've worked in the notebook so far. Now look at the same work from the UI.
1. Open **Monitoring > Spark** and select the warehouse **BANKING_WH**.
2. **Spark Sessions** lists your session, `de4_<your user>`, with you as the owner and its queries.
3. **Batch Jobs** lists `payments_nightly` (succeeded) and `payments_nightly_broken` (failed), with logs and the Telemetry trace.
Note: the clips in the earlier steps show what this screen looks like at that point in the lab.
steps.expect: your session and both batch runs listed, matching what you ran in the notebook
steps.mediaCaption: Monitoring > Spark > Select warehouse BANKING_WH > Spark Sessions

modules.check: Your Spark session is listed under your name, `PAYMENTS_CURRENT` matches the source, a `payments_nightly` batch job succeeded, a failed run is recorded, and `SPARK_JOB_FAILURE_ALERT` exists.
modules.note: Bring the Spark code, leave the clusters. The same PySpark runs on Snowflake warehouses against governed Iceberg and Snowflake tables, interactive or batch, and every session, job, log and trace is in one place: Monitoring > Spark.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- DE4: Spark on Snowflake - reference SQL
-- Run as HOL_PARTICIPANT. The PySpark itself is in de4_pipeline.py
-- (the batch job) and notebooks/de4_spark_on_snowflake.ipynb (interactive).
-- =====================================================
USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE4.1 The raw feed: duplicates, late arrivals and bad rows
-- -----------------------------------------------------
SELECT COUNT(*) AS EVENTS, COUNT(DISTINCT EVENT_ID) AS DISTINCT_EVENTS,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT EVENT_ID) AS DUPLICATE_DELIVERIES,
       COUNT_IF(PAYMENT_ID IS NULL) AS NO_PAYMENT_ID
FROM PAYMENT_STATUS_UPDATES;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE4.4 Run the pipeline as a batch job, straight from the lab's git repo.
-- No cluster: it runs on the session warehouse. The query ID is the job ID.
-- -----------------------------------------------------
EXECUTE CODE BUNDLE FROM '@BANKING_HOL_SETUP.PUBLIC.HOL_REPO/branches/main/vignettes/de4_spark_on_snowflake'
  ENTRYPOINT = 'de4_pipeline.py'
  ARGUMENTS = ('--schema', 'BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB', '--app-name', 'payments_nightly')
  EXECUTION_NAME = 'payments_nightly'
  WITH SPECIFICATION $$
bundle:
  type: spark
  compute_type: warehouse
  language: python
  compute_options: {}
$$;

SELECT * FROM PIPELINE_RECONCILIATION ORDER BY CHECKED_AT DESC;
SELECT REJECT_REASON, COUNT(*) AS ROWS_HELD FROM PAYMENT_UPDATES_QUARANTINE GROUP BY 1;
SELECT * FROM FAILED_PAYMENTS_BY_SCHEME ORDER BY PAYMENTS DESC;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE4.5 Schedule it: a task runs the same statement every night
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK PAYMENTS_NIGHTLY_SPARK
  WAREHOUSE = BANKING_WH
  SCHEDULE = 'USING CRON 0 2 * * * Europe/London'
  COMMENT = 'DE4: nightly PySpark payments pipeline'
AS
  EXECUTE CODE BUNDLE FROM '@BANKING_HOL_SETUP.PUBLIC.HOL_REPO/branches/main/vignettes/de4_spark_on_snowflake'
    ENTRYPOINT = 'de4_pipeline.py'
    ARGUMENTS = ('--schema', 'BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB', '--app-name', 'payments_nightly')
    EXECUTION_NAME = 'payments_nightly'
    WITH SPECIFICATION $$
bundle:
  type: spark
  compute_type: warehouse
  language: python
  compute_options: {}
$$;
ALTER TASK PAYMENTS_NIGHTLY_SPARK RESUME;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE4.6 Break it: upstream renamed the feed. The run fails, and the error
-- is in Monitoring > Spark > Batch Jobs (and CODE_BUNDLE_HISTORY).
-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- (wrapped so the expected failure doesn't stop the rest of this file; the reason is returned)
EXECUTE IMMEDIATE $$
BEGIN
  EXECUTE CODE BUNDLE FROM '@BANKING_HOL_SETUP.PUBLIC.HOL_REPO/branches/main/vignettes/de4_spark_on_snowflake'
    ENTRYPOINT = 'de4_pipeline.py'
    ARGUMENTS = ('--schema', 'BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB', '--source', 'PAYMENT_STATUS_UPDATES_V2', '--app-name', 'payments_nightly_broken')
    EXECUTION_NAME = 'payments_nightly_broken'
    WITH SPECIFICATION '
bundle:
  type: spark
  compute_type: warehouse
  language: python
  compute_options: {}
';
  RETURN 'Unexpected: the broken run succeeded';
EXCEPTION
  WHEN OTHER THEN RETURN 'Failed as intended: ' || LEFT(SQLERRM, 300);
END;
$$;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE4.7 The data behind Monitoring > Spark, as SQL
-- -----------------------------------------------------
SELECT NAME, MODE, OWNER, EXECUTION_STATUS, CREATED_ON,
       DATEDIFF('second', STARTED_ON, COMPLETED_ON) AS SECONDS, ERROR_CODE
FROM TABLE(SNOWFLAKE.SNOWPARK_CONNECT.GET_SPARK_APPLICATION_HISTORY(
    CREATION_TIME_START => DATEADD('day', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()), RESULT_LIMIT => 100))
ORDER BY CREATED_ON DESC;

-- why it failed: the job's ERROR logs in the event table
SELECT e.TIMESTAMP, e.RECORD['severity_text']::STRING AS SEVERITY, LEFT(e.VALUE::STRING, 300) AS MESSAGE
FROM SNOWFLAKE.TELEMETRY.EVENTS_VIEW e
WHERE e.TIMESTAMP > DATEADD('hour', -2, SYSDATE())
  AND e.RECORD_TYPE = 'LOG' AND e.RECORD['severity_text']::STRING IN ('ERROR', 'FATAL')
  AND e.RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES['snow.query.id']::STRING = (
      SELECT EXECUTE_QUERY_ID FROM TABLE(SNOWFLAKE.SNOWPARK_CONNECT.GET_SPARK_APPLICATION_HISTORY(RESULT_LIMIT => 100))
      WHERE NAME ILIKE '%payments_nightly_broken%' ORDER BY CREATED_ON DESC LIMIT 1)
ORDER BY e.TIMESTAMP;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- DE4.8 Alert on failed Spark jobs: every 5 minutes, record new failures
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS SPARK_JOB_FAILURES (
    APPLICATION_ID VARCHAR, NAME VARCHAR, MODE VARCHAR, OWNER VARCHAR,
    COMPLETED_ON TIMESTAMP_LTZ, ERROR_CODE VARCHAR, RECORDED_AT TIMESTAMP_LTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP());

CREATE OR REPLACE ALERT SPARK_JOB_FAILURE_ALERT
  WAREHOUSE = BANKING_WH
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
  IF (EXISTS (
    SELECT ID, NAME, MODE, OWNER, COMPLETED_ON, ERROR_CODE
    FROM TABLE(SNOWFLAKE.SNOWPARK_CONNECT.GET_SPARK_APPLICATION_HISTORY(
        CREATION_TIME_START => DATEADD('day', -1, SNOWFLAKE.ALERT.SCHEDULED_TIME()), RESULT_LIMIT => 10000))
    WHERE EXECUTION_STATUS = 'FAILED' AND MODE <> 'SCOS_CLIENT'
      AND ID NOT IN (SELECT APPLICATION_ID FROM BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB.SPARK_JOB_FAILURES)))
  THEN
    INSERT INTO BANKING_HOL.SPARK_LAB.SPARK_JOB_FAILURES (APPLICATION_ID, NAME, MODE, OWNER, COMPLETED_ON, ERROR_CODE)
    SELECT ID, NAME, MODE, OWNER, COMPLETED_ON, ERROR_CODE
    FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(SNOWFLAKE.ALERT.GET_CONDITION_QUERY_UUID()));
ALTER ALERT SPARK_JOB_FAILURE_ALERT RESUME;
EXECUTE ALERT SPARK_JOB_FAILURE_ALERT;  -- don't wait 5 minutes

SELECT * FROM SPARK_JOB_FAILURES ORDER BY RECORDED_AT DESC;

modules.title: Know where every file, model and app lives
modules.prerequisites: None. Step 5 lists the models from DS1, so press **Fast-forward** on DS1 first if you skipped it
modules.question: A fraud investigator needs the police report and the phishing screenshot for one case, a regulator asks which models are in production, and an auditor asks who can reach the evidence. Can we answer all three from one governed place, without files and models scattered across shared drives?
build: `EVIDENCE_CATALOGUE`: every evidence file on the stage, with its case and type
`EVIDENCE_SHARE`: a stage holding one case's files, readable by a role you choose
`PLATFORM_INVENTORY`: every stage and registered model with its owner

steps.title: Find where the files live
steps.body: Stages hold the files Snowflake works with: documents, images, notebooks and training code. Start by seeing what the lab has.
steps.prompt: List every stage in the database BANKING_HOL from BANKING_HOL.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.STAGES: schema, name, type and owner role. Then, for the stage BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.FINCRIME_EVIDENCE, show the file count and total size by file type from its directory table. Do not ask me questions.
steps.expect: six stages, and 150 evidence files across PDFs and PNG images

steps.title: Catalogue the evidence
steps.prompt: In BANKING_HOL.GOVERNANCE create a table EVIDENCE_CATALOGUE from DIRECTORY(@BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.FINCRIME_EVIDENCE): FILE_NAME (the relative path), CASE_ID (the part of the name before the first underscore), EVIDENCE_TYPE (the name without the case id and the file extension), FILE_FORMAT (PDF or PNG, upper case), SIZE_BYTES and LAST_MODIFIED. Then show the number of files per evidence type.
steps.expect: five evidence types: 50 police reports, 40 phishing texts, 31 booking confirmations, 19 damaged goods photos and 10 refund policy screenshots

steps.title: Read a file straight from the stage
steps.body: **Tip:** the file is not copied anywhere. The stage is the single copy, and your read permission decides who can run this.
steps.prompt: Use AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT in OCR mode on the file FRC100054_police_report.pdf in @BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.FINCRIME_EVIDENCE with TO_FILE, and show the first 400 characters of the text.
steps.expect: a crime reference, the date reported and the offence, read from the PDF

steps.title: Share one case with a role, and no more
steps.body: **Important:** run `USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE` first, or your other roles still give access and nothing is denied.
steps.prompt: In BANKING_HOL.GOVERNANCE create a stage EVIDENCE_SHARE with a directory table and Snowflake-managed encryption. Copy the files whose names contain FRC100054 from @BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.FINCRIME_EVIDENCE into it with COPY FILES, refresh the directory table, and grant READ on the stage to HOL_RESTRICTED. Then, after USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE and USE ROLE HOL_RESTRICTED, count the files in DIRECTORY(@BANKING_HOL.GOVERNANCE.EVIDENCE_SHARE) and in DIRECTORY(@BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.FINCRIME_EVIDENCE), showing the error if one fails. Switch back to HOL_PARTICIPANT at the end.
steps.expect: 2 files in `EVIDENCE_SHARE`, and "does not exist or is not authorized" for the full evidence stage

steps.title: Keep one inventory of stages and models
steps.body: Models live in the Model Registry, the same governed place as the data. One inventory shows both.
steps.prompt: In BANKING_HOL.GOVERNANCE create a table PLATFORM_INVENTORY (OBJECT_TYPE, OBJECT_NAME, OWNER_ROLE, DETAIL) from two sources with UNION ALL: every stage from BANKING_HOL.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.STAGES as 'Stage' (schema.name, owner, stage type), and every row of BANKING_HOL.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.MODEL_VERSIONS as 'Model version' (schema.model and version name, owner, and the model's functions as a comma-separated list). Show the count by OBJECT_TYPE.
steps.expect: stages and model versions, each with an owner role

steps.title: Answer the auditor
steps.prompt: Using BANKING_HOL.GOVERNANCE.PLATFORM_INVENTORY and SHOW GRANTS on the stage BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.FINCRIME_EVIDENCE, answer in plain English: which stages exist, which roles can read the evidence stage, which models are registered and who owns them. Then say what an auditor should ask next.
steps.expect: the evidence stage readable by `HOL_PARTICIPANT` and owned by `HOL_ADMIN`, and the attrition and margin models owned by the builder role

modules.check: `EVIDENCE_CATALOGUE` has 150 files, `EVIDENCE_SHARE` holds the two files of case FRC100054 and is readable by `HOL_RESTRICTED`, and `PLATFORM_INVENTORY` lists stages and model versions.
modules.note: Evidence, notebooks, training code and application artefacts sit on stages and in registries inside the same account as the data, so one set of roles governs all of them. Application and container images are held the same way, in image and artifact repositories. Lineage and access history, shown in GOV2, record who read each file.

modules.title: Interactive payments report with Cortex Code
modules.prerequisites: Core C1 only
modules.question: Can ops and RMs get the client 360 from C1 as a live, interactive report they can filter themselves, refreshed every morning?
build: An interactive, bank-branded HTML payments report, built by Cortex Code
Your own variation of it: new brand, charts or filters
A daily Cortex Code automation that rebuilds the report with fresh data

steps.title: Build an interactive report
steps.body:
1. Paste the prompt below into the **How can I help?** box.
2. Press **Allow** on each **Run this command?** card while it queries and builds.
3. Open the preview link Cortex Code gives you.
steps.where: the **CoCo** tab, in your C1 session or a **New session**
steps.prompt: Using the payments, accounts, customers, relationship managers and feedback tables in BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA, build an interactive HTML report of corporate payments health. Show headline figures, a monthly trend, a breakdown by payment type, and a sortable table of clients with their RM, failed payments and feedback. Let me filter by payment type, region and channel. Brand it as a UK bank (navy and cyan, red for failures). My role is read-only. Preview it and give me the link.
steps.expect: Cortex Code explores the tables, builds the report and gives you a preview link
steps.pasteInto: the **How can I help?** box in the **CoCo** tab
steps.mediaCaption: CoCo > New session, then paste the report prompt

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.body:
Now ask for your own changes, one prompt at a time. Some ideas:
- **Rebrand it:** "Re-skin the report in Snowflake brand colours: Snowflake Blue #29B5E8, Mid Blue #11567F, Midnight #000000."
- **Add a chart:** "Add a heatmap of failure rate by region and payment type."
- **Add a filter:** "Add a relationship manager filter that also filters the client table."
- **Explain the numbers:** "Add a short summary at the top of the three things ops should act on this week."
- **Make it for one audience:** "Make a one-page version for RMs that only shows their own clients."
1. Paste one idea, or write your own.
2. Open the new preview link and check the change.
3. Repeat until you're happy with it.
**Tip:** ask for one change at a time. If something breaks, say "undo the last change".
steps.expect: an updated preview after each prompt, with your changes and the totals unchanged

steps.title: Refresh the report every morning
steps.body:
The report embeds its data, so it shows the numbers from when it was built. A daily automation rebuilds it with fresh data.
1. Paste the prompt below.
2. Check the summary Cortex Code shows: name, schedule and read-only.
3. Let it run once now, so you can see the refreshed report.
4. Find it later under **Automations** in the CoCo side nav (below **New session**).
steps.prompt: Set up a daily Cortex Code automation called PAYMENTS_REPORT_REFRESH that runs at 07:00 Europe/London. Each run: re-run the queries behind the interactive payments report we just built, rebuild the same report with today's data, check the totals against BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA, and save it in the same place with today's date in the definitions section. It runs unattended, so it must not ask questions and must stay read-only. Create it paused, run it once now so I can see the result, then start the schedule.
steps.expect: Cortex Code summarises the automation, creates it paused, runs it once and shows the rebuilt report, then asks before starting the schedule. Each run uses your default role (`HOL_PARTICIPANT`).
steps.pasteInto: the **How can I help?** box in the **CoCo** tab
steps.mediaCaption: Your automations live under CoCo > Automations

modules.check: Your report preview opens, filters change the headline figures, and **Reset** brings them back to 50,000 payments.
modules.note: At a bank the same report would read from the governed data product views rather than RAW_DATA, and be shared through Snowflake Intelligence instead of a preview link.
modules.sql:
-- DA0: the totals the interactive report must match (Cortex Code builds the report itself).
-- Run as HOL_PARTICIPANT on BANKING_WH. Expect 50,000 payments and about 96% success; the exact counts differ per account (the data is generated at install).
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                       AS payments,
       COUNT_IF(STATUS = 'FAILED')                                    AS failed,
       COUNT_IF(STATUS = 'RETURNED')                                  AS returned,
       ROUND(100 * COUNT_IF(STATUS = 'COMPLETED') / COUNT(*), 2)      AS success_rate_pct,
       ROUND(SUM(IFF(CURRENCY = 'GBP', AMOUNT, AMOUNT * FX_RATE)) / 1e9, 1) AS gbp_volume_bn
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.PAYMENTS;

modules.title: AI SQL on customer feedback
modules.prerequisites: `setup/catchup/core_analytics.sql` (or DE1)
modules.question: What are corporate clients actually complaining about, by scheme and by relationship manager - without reading 2,000 comments?
build: `FEEDBACK_ENRICHED` (sentiment + topic)

steps.title: Open the starter notebook and create its service
steps.body:
1. Open `notebooks/` > **da1_feedback_analysis.ipynb** in the file explorer.
- Can't see `notebooks/` and `vignettes/`? You're in the wrong Workspace. Pick **banking-hol-pack** from the Workspace dropdown (top left).
2. In the notebook toolbar, click the arrow next to the status dot (right of the blue run button).
3. Choose **Create new service**.
- Already created one in another module? Pick it under **Select service** instead, usually `USER_SERVICE_1`.
4. Expand **Service settings** in **Connect your notebook** and fill it in as below. Only the three **bold** rows change.
| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Service name | leave the default (e.g. `USER_SERVICE_1`) |
| Artifact repositories | leave as is (`SNOWFLAKE.SNOWPARK.PYPI_SHARED_REPOSITORY`) |
| Enable distributed compute | off |
| Runtime | leave as is (v3.0 · Python 3.12) |
| Compute type | CPU |
| Custom image | leave empty |
| **Compute pool** | **NOTEBOOK_POOL** (change it from HOL_COMPUTE_POOL_CPU) |
| **Idle timeout** | **1 hour** (change it from 24 hours) |
| **External access integrations** | **HOL_NOTEBOOK_ACCESS_INTEGRATION** (lets notebooks reach Postgres and the AI Gateway; set it here so one service works for every notebook module) |
| Secrets | leave empty |
**Trial accounts:** there's no HOL_NOTEBOOK_ACCESS_INTEGRATION (trials don't allow external access). Leave **External access integrations** empty: this module works without it.
5. Click **Create and connect**. The first start takes 1-2 minutes.
6. Check the role is **HOL_PARTICIPANT** and the warehouse is **BANKING_WH** (role and warehouse button in the notebook toolbar).
The starter notebook has one numbered heading per step, so Cortex Code puts each cell in the right place.
A notebook runs on its own **notebook service**, which you create once.
SQL cells run on the warehouse. Python and charts run on the service.
You'll build this whole module as cells in this notebook: Cortex Code adds them, and you run each one.

steps.expect: the starter notebook open in banking-hol-pack with its numbered headings, and the status dot showing the service connected
