WITH v AS (
    SELECT v.*, f.PRODUCTS_HELD, f.ON_LEGACY_SAVER, f.SALARY_TREND, f.DIGITAL_ACTIVE, f.BRANCH_AT_RISK, f.SAVINGS_BALANCE,
           v.LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP >= PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v.LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP) OVER () AS HIGH_VALUE,
           v.CHURN_3M >= PERCENTILE_CONT(0.80) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY v.CHURN_3M) OVER () AS HIGH_RISK
    FROM CUSTOMER_VALUE v JOIN BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_CHURN_FEATURES f USING (CUSTOMER_ID))
SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP, VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP, CHURN_3M,
       CASE WHEN HIGH_VALUE AND HIGH_RISK THEN 'Save now'
            WHEN HIGH_VALUE THEN 'Grow'
            WHEN HIGH_RISK THEN 'Serve digitally'
            ELSE 'Maintain' END AS SEGMENT,
       CASE WHEN ON_LEGACY_SAVER = 1 THEN 'Move to a better savings rate'
            WHEN SALARY_TREND < 0.8 THEN 'Payment holiday or budgeting support'
            WHEN BRANCH_AT_RISK = 1 THEN 'Branch change: introduce digital and nearest branch'
            WHEN NOT DIGITAL_ACTIVE AND HIGH_RISK THEN 'App onboarding call'
            WHEN HIGH_VALUE AND HIGH_RISK THEN 'Retention call from a named adviser'
            WHEN HIGH_VALUE AND PRODUCTS_HELD <= 2 THEN 'Cross-sell: ISA or credit card'
            WHEN HIGH_VALUE AND SAVINGS_BALANCE >= 20000 THEN 'Premier upgrade'
            WHEN HIGH_VALUE THEN 'Thank-you: fee-free month'
            ELSE 'No action' END AS NEXT_BEST_OFFER
FROM v;
SELECT SEGMENT, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS, ROUND(SUM(LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP)) AS LIFETIME_VALUE, ROUND(SUM(VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP)) AS VALUE_AT_RISK
FROM CUSTOMER_VALUE_SEGMENTS GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY VALUE_AT_RISK DESC;

-- 5.
SELECT c.FIRST_NAME || ' ' || c.LAST_NAME AS CUSTOMER, c.CITY, v.LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP, v.VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP,
       ROUND(100 * v.CHURN_3M, 1) AS CHANCE_OF_LEAVING_PCT, v.NEXT_BEST_OFFER
FROM CUSTOMER_VALUE_SEGMENTS v JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c USING (CUSTOMER_ID)
WHERE v.SEGMENT = 'Save now'
ORDER BY v.VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP DESC LIMIT 20;

modules.title: Level of detail analysis in a semantic view
modules.persona: Data Analyst (Retail Banking), Tableau, Power BI and BI users
modules.prerequisites: DA5 (uses `ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE` and `CUSTOMER_VALUE_SEGMENTS`; to catch up, run `vignettes/da5_customer_value/da5.sql`)
modules.question: How does each neighbourhood, branch and segment compare with its city and with the UK, on profit per customer and on lifetime value at risk, from one set of definitions everyone shares?
build: View `ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL`: one row per retail customer with 12-month profit, lifetime value, value at risk and value segment
Semantic view `ANALYTICS.SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE` with **level of detail (LOD) metrics**: FIXED, INCLUDE and EXCLUDE, the same ideas as Tableau's LOD expressions
Agent `ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE_ADVISOR` that answers the same comparisons in plain English

steps.title: Open a SQL file
steps.body: 1. Name it `da6_level_of_detail.sql` and set the context:
steps.where: Snowsight > Projects > Workspaces > + Add new > SQL File, role HOL_PARTICIPANT, warehouse BANKING_WH

steps.title: One row per customer
steps.body: 1. Paste and run:
steps.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL
  COMMENT = 'DA6: one row per retail customer with 12-month profit, lifetime value (DA5) and city and UK benchmarks' AS
WITH base AS (
    SELECT c.CUSTOMER_ID, c.CITY, INITCAP(REPLACE(c.SEGMENT, '_', ' ')) AS SEGMENT, b.BRANCH_NAME,
           H3_LATLNG_TO_CELL_STRING(c.HOME_LAT, c.HOME_LON, 7) AS NEIGHBOURHOOD,
           p.PROFIT_12M_GBP, v.LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP, v.VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP,
           s.SEGMENT AS VALUE_SEGMENT, s.NEXT_BEST_OFFER
    FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c
    JOIN BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.BRANCHES b ON b.BRANCH_ID = c.HOME_BRANCH_ID
    JOIN (SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, SUM(PROFIT_GBP) AS PROFIT_12M_GBP
          FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT GROUP BY 1) p USING (CUSTOMER_ID)
    LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER_VALUE v USING (CUSTOMER_ID)
    LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER_VALUE_SEGMENTS s USING (CUSTOMER_ID))
-- the same benchmarks as plain columns, for tools that don't use LOD metrics yet (Cortex Analyst, agents)
SELECT *, ROUND(AVG(PROFIT_12M_GBP) OVER (PARTITION BY CITY), 2) AS CITY_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP,
          ROUND(AVG(PROFIT_12M_GBP) OVER (), 2) AS UK_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP
FROM base;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS, COUNT(LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP) AS WITH_LIFETIME_VALUE FROM CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL;
steps.expect: 20,000 customers, about 18,400 with a lifetime value (DS4 scored the customers still with the bank on 31 Aug 2026)

steps.title: Create the semantic view
steps.body:
Read the METRICS block before you run it: ordinary metrics first, then INCLUDE, FIXED and EXCLUDE, then the plain benchmarks for agents.
1. Paste and run:
steps.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE SEMANTIC VIEW SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
  TABLES (
    cust AS CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL PRIMARY KEY (CUSTOMER_ID)
      COMMENT = 'One row per retail customer: 12-month profit, lifetime value, value at risk',
    months AS BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT PRIMARY KEY (CUSTOMER_ID, MONTH)
      COMMENT = 'One row per customer per month')
  RELATIONSHIPS (months (CUSTOMER_ID) REFERENCES cust)
  FACTS (
    cust.profit AS PROFIT_12M_GBP, cust.ltv AS LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP, cust.var AS VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP, cust.one AS 1,
    cust.city_benchmark AS CITY_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP, cust.uk_benchmark AS UK_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP,
    months.month_profit AS PROFIT_GBP)
  DIMENSIONS (
    cust.customer_id AS CUSTOMER_ID, cust.city AS CITY, cust.segment AS SEGMENT,
    cust.branch AS BRANCH_NAME WITH SYNONYMS = ('home branch'),
    cust.neighbourhood AS NEIGHBOURHOOD WITH SYNONYMS = ('hexagon', 'area', 'H3 cell'),
    cust.value_segment AS VALUE_SEGMENT, cust.next_best_offer AS NEXT_BEST_OFFER,
    months.month AS MONTH)
  METRICS (
    -- ordinary metrics: grouped by whatever the query groups by
    cust.customers AS COUNT(cust.customer_id),
    cust.total_profit AS SUM(cust.profit),
    cust.profit_per_customer AS SUM(cust.profit) / COUNT(cust.customer_id),
    cust.lifetime_value AS SUM(cust.ltv),
    cust.value_at_risk AS SUM(cust.var),
    months.avg_profit_per_customer_month AS AVG(months.month_profit)
      COMMENT = 'Average of customer-months: NOT the same as average profit per customer',
    -- INCLUDE: work out each customer's total first, then average across customers
    avg_profit_per_customer AS AVG(SUM(months.month_profit) INCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.customer_id))
      COMMENT = 'Average 12-month profit per customer, whatever the query groups by',
    -- FIXED: the city's figures, next to every neighbourhood, branch or segment in it
    city_profit AS SUM(SUM(cust.profit) FIXED DIMENSIONS (cust.city)),
    city_customers AS SUM(SUM(cust.one) FIXED DIMENSIONS (cust.city)),
    city_profit_per_customer AS city_profit / city_customers,
    vs_city_pct AS 100 * (cust.profit_per_customer / city_profit_per_customer - 1)
      COMMENT = 'Profit per customer against the city average, in percent',
    -- EXCLUDE: drop every customer dimension, so this is the UK whatever the query groups by
    uk_profit AS SUM(SUM(cust.profit) EXCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.city, cust.segment, cust.branch, cust.neighbourhood, cust.value_segment, cust.next_best_offer)),
    uk_customers AS SUM(SUM(cust.one) EXCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.city, cust.segment, cust.branch, cust.neighbourhood, cust.value_segment, cust.next_best_offer)),
    uk_value_at_risk AS SUM(SUM(cust.var) EXCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.city, cust.segment, cust.branch, cust.neighbourhood, cust.value_segment, cust.next_best_offer)),
    uk_profit_per_customer AS uk_profit / uk_customers,
    vs_uk_pct AS 100 * (cust.profit_per_customer / uk_profit_per_customer - 1),
    share_of_uk_profit_pct AS 100 * cust.total_profit / uk_profit,
    share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct AS 100 * cust.value_at_risk / uk_value_at_risk,
    -- the same benchmarks from plain columns: what Cortex Analyst and agents can use today
    cust.city_profit_per_customer_benchmark AS AVG(cust.city_benchmark),
    cust.uk_profit_per_customer_benchmark AS AVG(cust.uk_benchmark))
  COMMENT = 'DA6: retail customer profit and value, with level of detail (LOD) metrics for city and UK comparisons';
SHOW SEMANTIC METRICS IN SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE;
steps.expect: the semantic view created, with about 20 metrics

steps.title: See the same view in Semantic Studio
steps.body:
Semantic Studio shows the same view as a file you can read and edit.
1. Select **SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE** to open it. It opens as a YAML file in Workspaces.
2. Find the `avg_profit_per_customer`, `city_profit_per_customer` and `uk_profit` metrics.
3. Select the **YAML** tab (or read the file) to see the LOD clause in the governed definition.
4. Select **Monitoring** to see which agent requests use these metrics.
**Important:** don't select **Deploy** yet. Deploy overwrites the live view with your local file. Read first, then close the file.

steps.title: Build a view in the UI instead
steps.body:
Use this when you want a view without writing SQL. The Autopilot wizard asks for a description, example questions and tables.
1. Select **Add new** > **Semantic View**.
2. Name the view `SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE_UI`, choose the schema `BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS`, and add a description.
3. Under context, pick **SQL Queries**, or upload a **YAML** specification, or a **Power BI** file if you have one.
4. Select the tables `ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL` and `RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT`, then select **Create and save**.
5. Open the view in Semantic Studio and add the city comparison by hand, or ask CoCo: *Add a metric that compares profit per customer with the city average, in percent.*
steps.expect: a generated view. Compare its metrics with the SQL version above. The SQL version has the LOD metrics, so use it when you need the FIXED and EXCLUDE comparisons.

steps.title: INCLUDE: per customer, not per customer-month
steps.body:
The classic BI mistake: averaging the monthly rows gives profit per customer-*month*. INCLUDE totals each customer first.
1. Paste and run:
steps.sql:
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.segment
    METRICS cust.customers, months.avg_profit_per_customer_month, avg_profit_per_customer)
ORDER BY avg_profit_per_customer DESC;
steps.expect: two very different numbers per segment. Premier customers make about £155 per customer-month but about £1,750 per customer a year. Only the second answers "what is a Premier customer worth?"

steps.title: FIXED: each branch against its city
steps.body:
1. Paste and run:
2. Now move the filter **inside** the semantic view clause and compare:
steps.sql:
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.branch
    METRICS cust.profit_per_customer, uk_profit_per_customer
    WHERE cust.city = 'Leeds');
steps.expect: "UK profit per customer" is now the Leeds figure. A WHERE inside `SEMANTIC_VIEW()` filters the data *before* the LOD calculation (like a context filter in Tableau); a WHERE outside filters the rows *after* it.

steps.title: EXCLUDE: shares of the UK
steps.body:
1. Paste and run:
2. The same by value segment (from DA5):
**Preview note:** ask for the city (FIXED) comparisons and the UK (EXCLUDE) comparisons in separate queries. In the preview, mixing the two in one query can return wrong numbers.
steps.sql:
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.value_segment
    METRICS cust.customers, cust.lifetime_value, share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct, vs_uk_pct)
ORDER BY share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct DESC;
steps.expect: **Save now** is a few percent of customers but about a third of the UK's value at risk.

steps.title: Neighbourhoods against their city
steps.body:
This is what the executive demo's lasso does by hand: an area against the rest of its city.
1. Paste and run:
steps.sql:
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.city, cust.neighbourhood
    METRICS cust.customers, cust.profit_per_customer, vs_city_pct)
WHERE city = 'London' AND customers >= 30
ORDER BY vs_city_pct DESC LIMIT 10;
steps.expect: London neighbourhoods (H3 hexagons) where customers are worth more than twice the London average

steps.title: Look at it in Semantic Studio
steps.body:
1. Open the semantic view and find the LOD metrics (`avg_profit_per_customer`, `city_profit_per_customer`, `uk_profit`).
2. Read their definitions next to the ordinary metrics: the LOD clause is part of the governed definition, so every tool that queries the view gets the same answer.
steps.where: Snowsight > **Catalog** > Database Explorer > BANKING_HOL > ANALYTICS > Semantic Views > **SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE**

steps.title: Ask an agent the same questions
steps.body:
Agents don't use LOD metrics yet: given only those, an agent works the city and UK averages out with its own SQL. The semantic view also carries the same benchmarks as plain metrics (`city_profit_per_customer_benchmark`, `uk_profit_per_customer_benchmark`), so the agent can use the governed figures.
1. Paste and run:
2. Open **Snowflake CoWork**, pick **Customer Value Advisor** and ask: *How much of the UK's value at risk sits in each city?*
steps.where: the same SQL file, then Snowflake CoWork
steps.sql:
CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE_ADVISOR
  COMMENT = 'DA6: answers customer profit and value questions, with city and UK comparisons'
  PROFILE = '{"display_name": "Customer Value Advisor", "color": "blue"}'
  FROM SPECIFICATION
  $$
  models:
    orchestration: auto
  instructions:
    response: >
      You help a UK retail bank's customer value team. Give numbers in pounds, round percentages to whole
      numbers, and always say what each figure is compared with (the city average or the UK average).
    orchestration: >
      Use the Analyst tool for every question. To compare an area, branch or segment with its city or the UK,
      use the city_profit_per_customer_benchmark and uk_profit_per_customer_benchmark metrics alongside
      profit_per_customer.
    sample_questions:
      - question: "Which Leeds branches have the highest profit per customer, against the Leeds and UK averages?"
      - question: "How much of the UK's value at risk sits in each city?"
      - question: "Which London neighbourhoods are most profitable per customer compared with London as a whole?"
  tools:
    - tool_spec:
        type: "cortex_analyst_text_to_sql"
        name: "Analyst"
        description: "Retail customers: 12-month profit, lifetime value and value at risk, by city, branch, neighbourhood, segment and value segment, with city and UK benchmarks."
  tool_resources:
    Analyst:
      semantic_view: "BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE"
      execution_environment:
        type: "warehouse"
        warehouse: "BANKING_WH"
  $$;
SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.DATA_AGENT_RUN('BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE_ADVISOR',
  $${"messages":[{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Which Leeds branches have the highest profit per customer, against the Leeds and UK averages?"}]}]}$$) AS RESPONSE;
steps.expect: the same Leeds figures as the FIXED step (about £213 for Leeds and £233 for the UK), with the agent's SQL using the benchmark metrics

modules.check: - `SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE` exists with INCLUDE, FIXED and EXCLUDE metrics - The Leeds branch comparison gives every branch the same city figure - `CUSTOMER_VALUE_ADVISOR` answers the Leeds question with the Leeds and UK averages
modules.note: - **Bring your Tableau or Power BI logic with you.** LOD expressions in a semantic view mean the "per customer", "against the region" and "share of total" logic lives once, in Snowflake, instead of in every workbook. Power BI DAX measures can be imported with Autopilot. - **Context filters still matter.** Decide where a filter belongs (inside the semantic view query, or after it) the same way you decide what is a context filter in Tableau. - **Agents next.** When Cortex Analyst and agents support LOD metrics, the benchmark columns can go: the agent will use the same LOD definitions as everyone else. - **Performance.** At scale, materialize the semantic view's busiest metrics so dashboards and agents don't recompute them on every question.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- VIGNETTE DA6: LEVEL OF DETAIL ANALYSIS IN A SEMANTIC VIEW   (~40 min)
-- Persona:  Data Analyst (Retail Banking), Tableau and BI users
-- Question: "How does each neighbourhood, branch and segment compare with its city
--            and the UK, from one set of shared definitions?"
-- Prereq:   DA5 (ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE, CUSTOMER_VALUE_SEGMENTS)
-- LOD metrics in semantic views are in preview; Cortex Analyst and agents don't use them yet.
-- Reference SQL for each step in README.md.
-- =====================================================

-- 1.
USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS;

-- 2.
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL
  COMMENT = 'DA6: one row per retail customer with 12-month profit, lifetime value (DA5) and city and UK benchmarks' AS
WITH base AS (
    SELECT c.CUSTOMER_ID, c.CITY, INITCAP(REPLACE(c.SEGMENT, '_', ' ')) AS SEGMENT, b.BRANCH_NAME,
           H3_LATLNG_TO_CELL_STRING(c.HOME_LAT, c.HOME_LON, 7) AS NEIGHBOURHOOD,
           p.PROFIT_12M_GBP, v.LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP, v.VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP,
           s.SEGMENT AS VALUE_SEGMENT, s.NEXT_BEST_OFFER
    FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c
    JOIN BANKING_HOL.RETAIL.BRANCHES b ON b.BRANCH_ID = c.HOME_BRANCH_ID
    JOIN (SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, SUM(PROFIT_GBP) AS PROFIT_12M_GBP
          FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT GROUP BY 1) p USING (CUSTOMER_ID)
    LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER_VALUE v USING (CUSTOMER_ID)
    LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER_VALUE_SEGMENTS s USING (CUSTOMER_ID))
-- the same benchmarks as plain columns, for tools that don't use LOD metrics yet (Cortex Analyst, agents)
SELECT *, ROUND(AVG(PROFIT_12M_GBP) OVER (PARTITION BY CITY), 2) AS CITY_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP,
          ROUND(AVG(PROFIT_12M_GBP) OVER (), 2) AS UK_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP
FROM base;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS, COUNT(LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP) AS WITH_LIFETIME_VALUE FROM CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL;

-- 3.
CREATE OR REPLACE SEMANTIC VIEW SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
  TABLES (
    cust AS CUSTOMER_VALUE_DETAIL PRIMARY KEY (CUSTOMER_ID)
      COMMENT = 'One row per retail customer: 12-month profit, lifetime value, value at risk',
    months AS BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT PRIMARY KEY (CUSTOMER_ID, MONTH)
      COMMENT = 'One row per customer per month')
  RELATIONSHIPS (months (CUSTOMER_ID) REFERENCES cust)
  FACTS (
    cust.profit AS PROFIT_12M_GBP, cust.ltv AS LIFETIME_VALUE_GBP, cust.var AS VALUE_AT_RISK_GBP, cust.one AS 1,
    cust.city_benchmark AS CITY_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP, cust.uk_benchmark AS UK_PROFIT_PER_CUSTOMER_GBP,
    months.month_profit AS PROFIT_GBP)
  DIMENSIONS (
    cust.customer_id AS CUSTOMER_ID, cust.city AS CITY, cust.segment AS SEGMENT,
    cust.branch AS BRANCH_NAME WITH SYNONYMS = ('home branch'),
    cust.neighbourhood AS NEIGHBOURHOOD WITH SYNONYMS = ('hexagon', 'area', 'H3 cell'),
    cust.value_segment AS VALUE_SEGMENT, cust.next_best_offer AS NEXT_BEST_OFFER,
    months.month AS MONTH)
  METRICS (
    -- ordinary metrics: grouped by whatever the query groups by
    cust.customers AS COUNT(cust.customer_id),
    cust.total_profit AS SUM(cust.profit),
    cust.profit_per_customer AS SUM(cust.profit) / COUNT(cust.customer_id),
    cust.lifetime_value AS SUM(cust.ltv),
    cust.value_at_risk AS SUM(cust.var),
    months.avg_profit_per_customer_month AS AVG(months.month_profit)
      COMMENT = 'Average of customer-months: NOT the same as average profit per customer',
    -- INCLUDE: work out each customer's total first, then average across customers
    avg_profit_per_customer AS AVG(SUM(months.month_profit) INCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.customer_id))
      COMMENT = 'Average 12-month profit per customer, whatever the query groups by',
    -- FIXED: the city's figures, next to every neighbourhood, branch or segment in it
    city_profit AS SUM(SUM(cust.profit) FIXED DIMENSIONS (cust.city)),
    city_customers AS SUM(SUM(cust.one) FIXED DIMENSIONS (cust.city)),
    city_profit_per_customer AS city_profit / city_customers,
    vs_city_pct AS 100 * (cust.profit_per_customer / city_profit_per_customer - 1)
      COMMENT = 'Profit per customer against the city average, in percent',
    -- EXCLUDE: drop every customer dimension, so this is the UK whatever the query groups by
    uk_profit AS SUM(SUM(cust.profit) EXCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.city, cust.segment, cust.branch, cust.neighbourhood, cust.value_segment, cust.next_best_offer)),
    uk_customers AS SUM(SUM(cust.one) EXCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.city, cust.segment, cust.branch, cust.neighbourhood, cust.value_segment, cust.next_best_offer)),
    uk_value_at_risk AS SUM(SUM(cust.var) EXCLUDE DIMENSIONS (cust.city, cust.segment, cust.branch, cust.neighbourhood, cust.value_segment, cust.next_best_offer)),
    uk_profit_per_customer AS uk_profit / uk_customers,
    vs_uk_pct AS 100 * (cust.profit_per_customer / uk_profit_per_customer - 1),
    share_of_uk_profit_pct AS 100 * cust.total_profit / uk_profit,
    share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct AS 100 * cust.value_at_risk / uk_value_at_risk,
    -- the same benchmarks from plain columns: what Cortex Analyst and agents can use today
    cust.city_profit_per_customer_benchmark AS AVG(cust.city_benchmark),
    cust.uk_profit_per_customer_benchmark AS AVG(cust.uk_benchmark))
  COMMENT = 'DA6: retail customer profit and value, with level of detail (LOD) metrics for city and UK comparisons';
SHOW SEMANTIC METRICS IN SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE;

-- 4.
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.segment
    METRICS cust.customers, months.avg_profit_per_customer_month, avg_profit_per_customer)
ORDER BY avg_profit_per_customer DESC;

-- 5.
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.city, cust.branch
    METRICS cust.customers, cust.profit_per_customer, city_profit_per_customer, vs_city_pct)
WHERE city = 'Leeds'
ORDER BY vs_city_pct DESC;

-- 6.
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.branch
    METRICS cust.profit_per_customer, uk_profit_per_customer
    WHERE cust.city = 'Leeds');

-- 7.
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.city
    METRICS cust.customers, cust.total_profit, share_of_uk_profit_pct, cust.value_at_risk, share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct)
ORDER BY share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct DESC;

-- 8.
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.value_segment
    METRICS cust.customers, cust.lifetime_value, share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct, vs_uk_pct)
ORDER BY share_of_uk_value_at_risk_pct DESC;

-- 9.
SELECT * FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(SV_CUSTOMER_VALUE
    DIMENSIONS cust.city, cust.neighbourhood
    METRICS cust.customers, cust.profit_per_customer, vs_city_pct)
WHERE city = 'London' AND customers >= 30
ORDER BY vs_city_pct DESC LIMIT 10;

-- 10.
CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.CUSTOMER_VALUE_ADVISOR
  COMMENT = 'DA6: answers customer profit and value questions, with city and UK comparisons'
  PROFILE = '{"display_name": "Customer Value Advisor", "color": "blue"}'
  FROM SPECIFICATION
  $$
  models:
    orchestration: auto
  instructions:
    response: >
      You help a UK retail bank's customer value team. Give numbers in pounds, round percentages to whole
      numbers, and always say what each figure is compared with (the city average or the UK average).

modules.title: Tour the retail data as a data scientist
modules.prerequisites: Facilitator setup complete
modules.question: What can we predict from the retail banking data, what does a good training set look like, and where are the traps?
build: Nothing yet: you tour the retail data product with Cortex Code as a data scientist (the labels, the features, the class balance and the leakage traps), then pick a model to build in DS1 or DS2.

steps.title: Open Cortex Code
steps.body:
1. At the top left of Snowsight, switch the toggle from **Home** to **CoCo**.
2. Close the **CoCo mode (preview)** pop-up if it appears.
3. Press **New session**.
4. Paste each prompt in this module into the **How can I help?** box.
When Cortex Code wants to run a query, it shows a **Run this command?** card:
- **Allow** lets it run
- **Skip** stops it
**Tip:** you're signed in as `HOL_PARTICIPANT`, with `BANKING_WH` and `BANKING_HOL` as your defaults. Cortex Code uses them, so you don't need to set a role or warehouse.
steps.where: Snowsight home page, the **Home / CoCo** toggle (top left) > **CoCo**
steps.expect: the Cortex Code screen with a **How can I help?** box
steps.mediaCaption: Home > CoCo, then paste DS0's first prompt

steps.title: Find the labels
steps.body: **Tip:** rare labels are normal in banking. Accuracy is a useless metric when 98% of customers stay.
steps.prompt: I'm a data scientist exploring the retail banking tables in BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA (the RB_ tables). Which columns could be targets for a model? For attrition (RB_CUSTOMERS.CHURNED and CHURN_DATE) and fraud (RB_TRANSACTIONS.IS_FRAUD and FRAUD_TYPE), show the rate, the counts and how they change by month, and say how imbalanced each one is.
steps.expect: about 9% of customers left over the year and about 0.4% of transactions are fraud, in four fraud types, so both labels are heavily imbalanced

steps.title: Meet the features
steps.prompt: For attrition, which signals in RB_CUSTOMERS, RB_ACCOUNTS joined to RB_PRODUCTS, RB_EMPLOYMENT and RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT look different for customers who left? Compare leavers with stayers on tenure, product count, savings rate (and legacy savings products), salary trend, app logins, branch visits, home branch and complaints. Show it as one table.
steps.expect: leavers have shorter tenure (about 59 months against 89), fewer products and three times the complaints, and are five times as likely to be branch-reliant at one of the three closure branches. Low-rate legacy savers only stand out when the balance is large.

steps.title: Spot the leakage
steps.body: **Important:** a model that sees the future looks brilliant in training and fails in production.
steps.prompt: If I train an attrition model on these tables, which columns would leak the answer? Check CHURN_DATE, CHURN_REASON, RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT.CHURNED_FLAG, RB_ACCOUNTS.CLOSED_DATE and STATUS, and the snapshot months just before a customer leaves. Explain how to build point-in-time features from an observation date, so the model only sees what we knew at the time.
steps.expect: all of those columns leak, and so do the last months before leaving, when salary credits fade. The fix is one observation date (for example 31 Aug 2026), features only from before it, and the label from the 3 months after.

steps.title: See what fraud looks like
steps.prompt: For RB_TRANSACTIONS, profile the four fraud types: typical amount, hour of day, online or not, new payee, merchant country and how quickly the transactions follow each other. What features would an anomaly detector need, given we can't rely on labels for new fraud patterns?
steps.expect: card testing is a burst of tiny online payments then a big one; impossible travel is two countries within an hour; account takeover is night-time transfers to new payees; APP scams are large Faster Payments to new payees, often from older customers

steps.title: Pick your model
steps.body:
- **DS1** trains the attrition model in a notebook, tracks it in an experiment and registers it
- **DS2** builds the fraud anomaly model the same way
steps.prompt: Summarise what we found as a short modelling brief for two models: an attrition classifier (target, observation window, features, leakage to avoid, metric) and a fraud anomaly detector (features, how to evaluate without trusting labels). Which tables would each read?
steps.expect: a two-part brief. Then build them:

modules.check: You have profiled the retail labels and features, including the monthly snapshot and the transaction ledger.
modules.note: At a bank a model like this goes through model risk review. Point-in-time features, a tracked experiment and a registered, versioned model are the evidence that review asks for.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- DS0: TOUR THE RETAIL DATA AS A DATA SCIENTIST - reference queries
-- Run as HOL_PARTICIPANT.
-- =====================================================
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;

-- 1. The labels and how imbalanced they are
SELECT 'attrition (customers who left)' AS LABEL, COUNT_IF(CHURNED) AS POSITIVES, COUNT(*) AS TOTAL,
       ROUND(100 * COUNT_IF(CHURNED) / COUNT(*), 2) AS PCT FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS
UNION ALL
SELECT 'fraud (transactions)', COUNT_IF(IS_FRAUD), COUNT(*), ROUND(100 * COUNT_IF(IS_FRAUD) / COUNT(*), 2)
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_TRANSACTIONS;

-- 2. Leavers against stayers
SELECT c.CHURNED,
       ROUND(AVG(DATEDIFF(month, c.CUSTOMER_SINCE, '2026-11-20'::DATE))) AS AVG_TENURE_MONTHS,
       ROUND(AVG(h.PRODUCTS), 2) AS AVG_PRODUCTS,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(h.LEGACY_SAVER), 1) AS PCT_LEGACY_SAVER,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(IFF(c.HOME_BRANCH_ID IN ('BR-MAN-90', 'BR-LDS-90', 'BR-CDF-90') AND NOT c.DIGITAL_ACTIVE, 1, 0)), 1) AS PCT_BRANCH_RELIANT_AT_CLOSURE,
       ROUND(AVG(c.COMPLAINTS_12M), 2) AS AVG_COMPLAINTS
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c
JOIN (SELECT a.CUSTOMER_ID, COUNT(*) AS PRODUCTS, MAX(IFF(p.TIER = 'LEGACY', 1, 0)) AS LEGACY_SAVER
      FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_ACCOUNTS a JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_PRODUCTS p ON p.PRODUCT_ID = a.PRODUCT_ID
      GROUP BY 1) h ON h.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
GROUP BY 1;

-- 3. Leakage: salary credits fade in the months before a customer leaves
SELECT DATEDIFF(month, s.MONTH, c.CHURN_DATE) AS MONTHS_BEFORE_LEAVING, ROUND(AVG(s.SALARY_IN_GBP)) AS AVG_SALARY_IN
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT s
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c ON c.CUSTOMER_ID = s.CUSTOMER_ID
WHERE c.CHURNED AND DATEDIFF(month, s.MONTH, c.CHURN_DATE) BETWEEN 0 AND 6
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1 DESC;

-- 4. What each fraud type looks like
SELECT FRAUD_TYPE, COUNT(*) AS TXNS, ROUND(MEDIAN(-AMOUNT_GBP), 2) AS MEDIAN_AMOUNT,
       ROUND(AVG(HOUR(TXN_TS)), 1) AS AVG_HOUR, ROUND(100 * AVG(IFF(IS_ONLINE, 1, 0))) AS PCT_ONLINE,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(IFF(IS_NEW_PAYEE, 1, 0))) AS PCT_NEW_PAYEE, ROUND(100 * AVG(IFF(MERCHANT_COUNTRY <> 'GB', 1, 0))) AS PCT_ABROAD
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_TRANSACTIONS
WHERE IS_FRAUD GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;

steps.prompt: In the open notebook ds1_attrition_model, put each cell I ask for under its matching numbered heading. Under heading 1, add a SQL cell named features that creates the view BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_CHURN_FEATURES with one row per retail customer who was still a customer on the observation date 31 Aug 2026. Use only data from on or before that date: tenure, age, segment, IMD decile, housing tenure, credit score, digital active, whether their home branch is one of BR-MAN-90, BR-LDS-90 or BR-CDF-90, drive minutes to it, and from RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT the last 3 months' average logins, branch visits and card spend, latest balances and products held, salary trend (last 3 months against the 3 before), and from RB_ACCOUNTS joined to RB_PRODUCTS the lowest savings rate and whether they hold £15,000 or more on a legacy saver. The label CHURNED_NEXT_3M is 1 if CHURN_DATE falls in the 3 months after the observation date. Don't use CHURNED, CHURN_REASON, CHURNED_FLAG, CLOSED_DATE or STATUS. steps.title: Train two models and track them in an experiment
steps.body:
**Tip:** the first job takes a few minutes while DS_TRAINING_POOL starts. The notebook stays responsive: it only waits for the result.
Then compare the runs:
1. Open **AI & ML > Experiments** in Snowsight (in a new browser tab).
2. Open **RB_ATTRITION**, tick both runs and press **Compare**.
**Tip:** accuracy would be about 98% for a model that predicts nobody leaves. Lift in the top decile is what the retention team cares about.
steps.prompt: Under heading 2, add a Python cell named load that shows the row count and label balance of RB_CHURN_FEATURES with the active Snowpark session (don't pull it into pandas here). Then add a cell named train_and_track that first sets the session's database and schema to BANKING_HOL.ML (an ML Job needs them), then runs the training as a Snowflake ML Job, using the @remote decorator from snowflake.ml.jobs with compute pool DS_TRAINING_POOL and stage BANKING_HOL.ML.JOB_STAGE, so the training data and models never sit in this notebook's memory. Inside the job function: get the session with get_active_session, read RB_CHURN_FEATURES into pandas, split 70/30 stratified, and train a logistic regression baseline (balanced class weights, scaled features) and an XGBoost classifier (scale_pos_weight for the imbalance) as scikit-learn pipelines. Track each as a run in the Snowflake experiment RB_ATTRITION in BANKING_HOL.ML with snowflake.ml.experiment.ExperimentTracking, logging parameters including the observation date, and metrics AUC, average precision, precision in the top decile and lift in the top decile, with a unique timestamped run name each. Then log the best run's pipeline to the Model Registry in BANKING_HOL.ML as RB_ATTRITION_MODEL (metrics, sample input, target platform WAREHOUSE, a comment naming the experiment), let it generate the version name, make it the default, and return the metrics. Submit the job, wait for it, and print its status and result. Run both cells.
steps.expect: the job finishes as DONE with two runs in the experiment. Both score an AUC of about 0.83 to 0.87, XGBoost slightly ahead, and the top decile holds about 7 times the average rate of leavers.
steps.mediaCaption: Machine learning > Experiments > RB_ATTRITION > tick both runs > Compare

steps.mediaCaption: Machine learning > Models > RB_ATTRITION_MODEL

steps.title: Score every customer

Then add a SQL cell named risk_bands showing, per band, the customer count, average probability and the actual share who left. Run both.
steps.expect: about 900 HIGH, 2,800 MEDIUM and 14,800 LOW customers. About a third of the HIGH band really did leave, against about 2% overall.

steps.title: Explain the drivers

Then add a SQL cell named retention_list that joins RB_ATTRITION_SCORES to RB_CUSTOMERS and RETAIL.BRANCHES for the 20 HIGH-risk customers with the highest probability: name, city, home branch, products held and a suggested retention action for each. Run both.
steps.expect: the top drivers include complaints, short tenure, falling salary credits and branch reliance at a closure branch, then a call list of 20 customers with an action each

modules.note: At a bank a model like this goes to model risk review before anyone acts on it. Here, the review evidence comes built in: the experiment holds every run that was tried, the registry holds the exact version that scored customers, and lineage links the two.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- DS1: PREDICT ATTRITION - reference SQL
-- Point-in-time features for the attrition model: what we knew about each customer on
-- 31 Aug 2026, and whether they left in the 3 months after. Run as HOL_PARTICIPANT.
-- The notebook (notebooks/ds1_attrition_model.ipynb) trains on this view; this file is
-- the fallback and the answer key.
-- =====================================================
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ML;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW RB_CHURN_FEATURES COMMENT = 'DS1 point-in-time attrition features, observed 2026-08-31, label = left by 2026-11-30' AS
WITH obs AS (SELECT '2026-08-31'::DATE AS OBS_DATE),
snap AS (  -- only months up to the observation date: no peeking at the future
    SELECT s.CUSTOMER_ID,
           AVG(IFF(s.MONTH >  DATEADD(month, -3, o.OBS_DATE), s.SALARY_IN_GBP, NULL)) AS SALARY_L3M,
           AVG(IFF(s.MONTH <= DATEADD(month, -3, o.OBS_DATE), s.SALARY_IN_GBP, NULL)) AS SALARY_P3M,
           AVG(IFF(s.MONTH >  DATEADD(month, -3, o.OBS_DATE), s.APP_LOGINS, NULL))    AS LOGINS_L3M,
           AVG(IFF(s.MONTH >  DATEADD(month, -3, o.OBS_DATE), s.BRANCH_VISITS, NULL)) AS BRANCH_VISITS_L3M,
           AVG(IFF(s.MONTH >  DATEADD(month, -3, o.OBS_DATE), s.CARD_SPEND_GBP, NULL)) AS CARD_SPEND_L3M,
           MAX_BY(s.CURRENT_BALANCE_GBP, s.MONTH) AS CURRENT_BALANCE,
           MAX_BY(s.SAVINGS_BALANCE_GBP, s.MONTH) AS SAVINGS_BALANCE,
           MAX_BY(s.PRODUCTS_HELD, s.MONTH)       AS PRODUCTS_HELD,
           SUM(s.PROFIT_GBP)                      AS PROFIT_TO_DATE
    FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT s, obs o
    WHERE s.MONTH <= o.OBS_DATE
    GROUP BY s.CUSTOMER_ID
),
sav AS (
    SELECT a.CUSTOMER_ID, MIN(a.INTEREST_RATE_PCT) AS MIN_SAVINGS_RATE,
           -- £15k+ sitting on a closed, low-rate legacy saver: the rate-sensitive savers who leave
           MAX(IFF(p.TIER = 'LEGACY' AND a.BALANCE_GBP >= 15000, 1, 0)) AS ON_LEGACY_SAVER
    FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_ACCOUNTS a JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_PRODUCTS p ON p.PRODUCT_ID = a.PRODUCT_ID, obs o
    WHERE p.PRODUCT_FAMILY = 'SAVINGS' AND a.OPENED_DATE <= o.OBS_DATE
    GROUP BY a.CUSTOMER_ID
)
SELECT c.CUSTOMER_ID,
       DATEDIFF(month, c.CUSTOMER_SINCE, o.OBS_DATE) AS TENURE_MONTHS,
       c.AGE, c.SEGMENT, c.IMD_DECILE, c.HOUSING_TENURE, c.CREDIT_SCORE,
       IFF(c.DIGITAL_ACTIVE, 1, 0) AS DIGITAL_ACTIVE,
       IFF(c.HOME_BRANCH_ID IN ('BR-MAN-90', 'BR-LDS-90', 'BR-CDF-90'), 1, 0) AS BRANCH_AT_RISK,
       c.HOME_BRANCH_DRIVE_S / 60 AS BRANCH_DRIVE_MIN,
       s.PRODUCTS_HELD, s.CURRENT_BALANCE, s.SAVINGS_BALANCE, s.CARD_SPEND_L3M, s.LOGINS_L3M, s.BRANCH_VISITS_L3M,
       s.SALARY_L3M / NULLIF(s.SALARY_P3M, 0) AS SALARY_TREND,  -- below 1: pay starting to go elsewhere
       COALESCE(sv.MIN_SAVINGS_RATE, 0) AS MIN_SAVINGS_RATE, COALESCE(sv.ON_LEGACY_SAVER, 0) AS ON_LEGACY_SAVER,
       s.PROFIT_TO_DATE,
       -- the label: left in the 3 months after the observation date
       IFF(c.CHURN_DATE > o.OBS_DATE AND c.CHURN_DATE <= DATEADD(month, 3, o.OBS_DATE), 1, 0) AS CHURNED_NEXT_3M
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c
JOIN snap s ON s.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
LEFT JOIN sav sv ON sv.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
CROSS JOIN obs o
WHERE c.CUSTOMER_SINCE <= o.OBS_DATE
  AND (c.CHURN_DATE IS NULL OR c.CHURN_DATE > o.OBS_DATE);  -- still a customer on the observation date

-- Class balance: about 2-3% leave in the next 3 months
SELECT CHURNED_NEXT_3M, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS, ROUND(RATIO_TO_REPORT(COUNT(*)) OVER () * 100, 1) AS PCT
FROM RB_CHURN_FEATURES GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- Leakage traps to leave out: CHURN_DATE, CHURN_REASON, CHURNED, RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT.CHURNED_FLAG,
-- any snapshot month after OBS_DATE, RB_ACCOUNTS.CLOSED_DATE and STATUS.

-- After the notebook: the experiment, the registered model and the scores
SHOW EXPERIMENTS IN SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ML;
SHOW MODELS IN SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ML;
SELECT RISK_BAND, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS FROM BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_ATTRITION_SCORES GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

steps.title: Train anomaly models without labels and track them
steps.body:
**Tip:** the job runs on DS_TRAINING_POOL, not your notebook service. The first one takes a few minutes while the pool starts.
**Important:** the labels never touch training. They're only there to tell you whether the model would have caught real fraud.
steps.prompt: Under heading 2, add a Python cell named train_and_track that first sets the session's database and schema to BANKING_HOL.ML (an ML Job needs them), then runs the training as a Snowflake ML Job, using the @remote decorator from snowflake.ml.jobs with compute pool DS_TRAINING_POOL and stage BANKING_HOL.ML.JOB_STAGE, so the sample and models never sit in this notebook's memory. Inside the job function: get the session with get_active_session, sample 300,000 rows of RB_TXN_FEATURES, and train two scikit-learn IsolationForest models on the features only (no labels): 100 trees with contamination 0.005, and 300 trees with contamination 0.01. Track each as a run in the Snowflake experiment RB_FRAUD in BANKING_HOL.ML with ExperimentTracking, using unique timestamped run names. Score with -score_samples, flag the top 0.5% as alerts, and log the parameters, AUC and average precision against IS_FRAUD, precision and recall at the 0.5% alert rate, and recall for each FRAUD_TYPE. Then log the run with the best average precision to the Model Registry in BANKING_HOL.ML as RB_FRAUD_ANOMALY (sample input, metrics, target platform WAREHOUSE, a comment saying it was trained without labels), make it the default version, and return the metrics. Submit the job, wait for it, and print its status and result. Run it.
steps.expect: both runs score an AUC of about 0.99 against the labels. At a 0.5% alert rate, about 6 in 10 alerts are real fraud and about 2 in 3 to 3 in 4 frauds are caught: nearly all APP scams and account takeovers, most card testing, but only about 1 in 8 impossible-travel payments.

steps.title: Register and score every transaction
steps.prompt: Under heading 3, add a Python cell named register_and_score that gets the default version of RB_FRAUD_ANOMALY from the Model Registry in BANKING_HOL.ML, runs it with score_samples on a Snowpark DataFrame of every row of RB_TXN_FEATURES (so the scoring runs in the warehouse, not the notebook) and saves the top 0.5% most anomalous transactions to the table BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_FRAUD_ALERTS with TXN_ID, CUSTOMER_ID, TXN_TS and ANOMALY_SCORE. Then add a SQL cell named alerts_by_type counting the alerts by FRAUD_TYPE (null means not labelled fraud). Run both.
steps.expect: about 6,000 alerts, about 3,800 of them labelled fraud. The rest are unusual but genuine payments, which the fraud team would clear.

steps.title: Find what the model misses
steps.body: **Tip:** the alerts link to the fraud case notes, SAR narratives and evidence files in AI4, where AI SQL reads them.
steps.prompt: Under heading 4, add a SQL cell named misses that shows the fraud the model didn't flag, by FRAUD_TYPE, and explains why impossible travel slips through when each payment looks normal on its own. Then test a simple rule, COUNTRY_CHANGE_2H = 1, on its own: how many transactions it flags and how many are impossible travel. Suggest how to combine the model and the rule.
steps.expect: most of the missed fraud is impossible travel. The country-change rule flags about 2,100 transactions, about 300 of them impossible travel. Models and rules work best together.

modules.check: An experiment with at least two runs, a registered anomaly model and the alerts table all exist in `BANKING_HOL.ML`.
modules.note: Fraud models change often, so the registry's versions and the experiment's runs are how a bank shows which model was live when a payment was stopped, and why it was chosen.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- DS2: FRAUD ANOMALY DETECTION - reference SQL
-- Per-transaction behavioural features for an unsupervised anomaly model. Labels
-- (IS_FRAUD, FRAUD_TYPE) are kept only to evaluate it. Run as HOL_PARTICIPANT.
-- The notebook (notebooks/ds2_fraud_anomaly.ipynb) trains on this view.
-- =====================================================
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ML;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW RB_TXN_FEATURES COMMENT = 'DS2 behavioural features per outgoing retail transaction; IS_FRAUD kept for evaluation only' AS
WITH t AS (
    SELECT TXN_ID, CUSTOMER_ID, TXN_TS, -AMOUNT_GBP AS AMOUNT, CHANNEL, CATEGORY, MERCHANT_COUNTRY,
           IS_ONLINE, IS_NEW_PAYEE, IS_FRAUD, FRAUD_TYPE
    FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_TRANSACTIONS
    WHERE AMOUNT_GBP < 0  -- money going out
),
usual AS (
    SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, MEDIAN(AMOUNT) AS MEDIAN_AMOUNT, STDDEV(AMOUNT) AS SD_AMOUNT
    FROM t GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT t.TXN_ID, t.CUSTOMER_ID, t.TXN_TS,
       LN(1 + t.AMOUNT) AS LOG_AMOUNT,
       t.AMOUNT / NULLIF(u.MEDIAN_AMOUNT, 0) AS AMOUNT_VS_USUAL,  -- how unusual for this customer
       HOUR(t.TXN_TS) AS HOUR_OF_DAY,
       IFF(HOUR(t.TXN_TS) BETWEEN 0 AND 5, 1, 0) AS IS_NIGHT,
       IFF(t.IS_ONLINE, 1, 0) AS IS_ONLINE,
       IFF(t.IS_NEW_PAYEE, 1, 0) AS IS_NEW_PAYEE,
       IFF(t.MERCHANT_COUNTRY <> 'GB', 1, 0) AS IS_ABROAD,
       IFF(t.CHANNEL = 'FPS_OUT', 1, 0) AS IS_FASTER_PAYMENT,
       -- velocity: this customer's payments in the 30 minutes before
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY t.CUSTOMER_ID ORDER BY t.TXN_TS
                      RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '30 minutes' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) - 1 AS TXNS_PRIOR_30M,
       -- impossible travel: a different country within 2 hours
       IFF(LAG(t.MERCHANT_COUNTRY) OVER (PARTITION BY t.CUSTOMER_ID ORDER BY t.TXN_TS) <> t.MERCHANT_COUNTRY
           AND DATEDIFF(minute, LAG(t.TXN_TS) OVER (PARTITION BY t.CUSTOMER_ID ORDER BY t.TXN_TS), t.TXN_TS) <= 120, 1, 0) AS COUNTRY_CHANGE_2H,
       IFF(c.AGE >= 65, 1, 0) AS CUSTOMER_65_PLUS,
       IFF(t.IS_FRAUD, 1, 0) AS IS_FRAUD, t.FRAUD_TYPE  -- evaluation only, never a feature
FROM t
JOIN usual u ON u.CUSTOMER_ID = t.CUSTOMER_ID
JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_CUSTOMERS c ON c.CUSTOMER_ID = t.CUSTOMER_ID;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS TXNS, SUM(IS_FRAUD) AS FRAUD, ROUND(100 * AVG(IS_FRAUD), 2) AS FRAUD_PCT FROM RB_TXN_FEATURES;

-- After the notebook: how many of the flagged transactions are labelled fraud, by type
SELECT f.FRAUD_TYPE, COUNT(*) AS FLAGGED
FROM BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_FRAUD_ALERTS a JOIN RB_TXN_FEATURES f ON f.TXN_ID = a.TXN_ID
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
SHOW MODELS LIKE 'RB_FRAUD_ANOMALY' IN SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ML;

modules.title: Model risk evidence pack
modules.prerequisites: DS1, or `setup/catchup/ds1_model.sql`
modules.question: Model risk will ask what this model is, who owns it, what it may be used for, how well it really works, why we picked it over the alternative, and who approved it. Can we answer from the platform the model runs on, instead of a slide deck that's out of date by the next release?
build: `ML.MODEL_INVENTORY` from the Model Registry, with owner, permitted use, risk tier and status
`ML.MODEL_VALIDATION` (predicted vs actual leavers) and `ML.MODEL_CHALLENGERS` (every experiment run)
`ML.MODEL_CARD` drafted by AI from that evidence, and `ML.MODEL_APPROVALS` with the decision and its conditions

steps.title: Put the model on the inventory
steps.prompt: Run SHOW VERSIONS IN MODEL BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_ATTRITION_MODEL, then create a table BANKING_HOL.ML.MODEL_INVENTORY from its result (RESULT_SCAN of LAST_QUERY_ID) with MODEL_NAME, VERSION, IS_DEFAULT, PURPOSE (the version comment), FRAMEWORK (from model_attributes), AUC (from metadata metrics), REGISTERED_ON, and these fixed values cast to VARCHAR: OWNER 'Retail Analytics', PERMITTED_USE 'Rank customers for retention offers; never used to refuse a product or set a price', RISK_TIER 'MEDIUM', TRAINING_DATA 'ML.RB_CHURN_FEATURES (observed 2026-08-31, label: left by 2026-11-30)', STATUS 'PENDING_VALIDATION'. Show it.
steps.expect: one row per registered version, with the registry's own metrics next to what model risk needs

steps.title: Validate it against what really happened
steps.prompt: Create a table BANKING_HOL.ML.MODEL_VALIDATION comparing the model's average CHURN_PROBABILITY in ML.RB_ATTRITION_SCORES with the actual leave rate (CHURNED_NEXT_3M in ML.RB_CHURN_FEATURES), as percentages, with columns CUT, GROUP_NAME, CUSTOMERS, PREDICTED_PCT and ACTUAL_PCT: one set of rows by RISK_BAND and one by SEGMENT. Show it, and tell me in two sentences whether the model ranks customers well and whether its probabilities can be taken at face value.
steps.expect: the high band leaves far more often than the low band (it ranks well), but the predicted rates sit well above the actual ones (balanced class weights inflate them)

steps.title: Compare the champion with the challenger
steps.prompt: Run SHOW RUN METRICS IN EXPERIMENT BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_ATTRITION and pivot it into a table BANKING_HOL.ML.MODEL_CHALLENGERS with one row per run (RUN_NAME, AUC, AVG_PRECISION, LIFT_TOP_DECILE, PRECISION_TOP_DECILE). Mark which run is the registered default (its name starts the default version's comment in MODEL_INVENTORY) and explain the trade-off between the two runs.
steps.expect: two runs; the one with the higher AUC isn't necessarily the one with the best lift in the top decile, which is the number a retention team acts on

steps.title: Draft the model card
steps.prompt: Create a table BANKING_HOL.ML.MODEL_CARD with one row for the default version in MODEL_INVENTORY: MODEL_NAME, VERSION, DRAFTED_AT and CARD, a plain-English model card under 200 words written by AI_COMPLETE (claude-sonnet-4-5) from MODEL_INVENTORY, MODEL_VALIDATION and MODEL_CHALLENGERS only, as labelled lines: Purpose, Permitted use, Data, Performance, Champion vs challenger, Known limitations, Conditions for use. Show the card.
steps.expect: a card that says what the evidence says, including the calibration limitation

steps.title: Record the decision
steps.prompt: Create a table BANKING_HOL.ML.MODEL_APPROVALS (MODEL_NAME, VERSION, DECISION, CONDITIONS, APPROVER, DECIDED_AT) and insert a row for the default version: decision APPROVED_WITH_CONDITIONS, conditions 'Use for ranking only: probabilities run high against actual outcomes, so recalibrate before quoting them. Review quarterly.', approver CURRENT_USER(). Then update MODEL_INVENTORY.STATUS from the decision and show the inventory with the approval.
steps.expect: the inventory now says who approved the model, when, and on what conditions

modules.check: `MODEL_INVENTORY` shows `RB_ATTRITION_MODEL` as `APPROVED_WITH_CONDITIONS`, and `MODEL_VALIDATION` and `MODEL_CARD` explain why.
modules.note: SS1/23 sets the PRA's expectations for UK banks with internal-model approval for regulatory capital, across all their model types, and expects validation to be independent of the people who built the model. In production the inventory would cover every model, read straight from the registry, and monitoring would add drift over time. The executive demo's "Every model on the record" stop is this module, finished.
modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- DS3: Model risk evidence pack (solution / catch-up)
-- The PRA's SS1/23 principles (model identification, governance, development and use,
-- independent validation, risk mitigants) applied to the DS1 attrition model: an inventory
-- from the Model Registry, validation against what really happened, champion vs challenger
-- from the experiment, an AI-drafted model card, and a recorded approval.
-- Run as HOL_PARTICIPANT after DS1 (or setup/catchup/ds1_model.sql).
-- =====================================================
USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ML;

-- 1. Inventory: every version of every model in the registry, plus what model risk asks for
SHOW VERSIONS IN MODEL RB_ATTRITION_MODEL;
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE MODEL_INVENTORY AS
SELECT "model_name" AS MODEL_NAME, "name" AS VERSION, "is_default_version"::BOOLEAN AS IS_DEFAULT, "comment" AS PURPOSE,
       PARSE_JSON("model_attributes"):framework::VARCHAR AS FRAMEWORK,
       PARSE_JSON("metadata"):metrics:auc::FLOAT AS AUC,
       "created_on"::TIMESTAMP_LTZ AS REGISTERED_ON,
       'Retail Analytics' AS OWNER,
       'Rank customers for retention offers; never used to refuse a product or set a price' AS PERMITTED_USE,
       'MEDIUM' AS RISK_TIER,
       'ML.RB_CHURN_FEATURES (observed 2026-08-31, label: left by 2026-11-30)' AS TRAINING_DATA,
       'PENDING_VALIDATION'::VARCHAR AS STATUS
FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID()));
SELECT * FROM MODEL_INVENTORY;

-- 2. Validation: predicted vs actual, by risk band and by segment
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE MODEL_VALIDATION AS
WITH s AS (
  SELECT f.SEGMENT, sc.RISK_BAND, sc.CHURN_PROBABILITY, f.CHURNED_NEXT_3M
  FROM RB_ATTRITION_SCORES sc JOIN RB_CHURN_FEATURES f USING (CUSTOMER_ID))
SELECT 'RISK_BAND' AS CUT, RISK_BAND AS GROUP_NAME, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMERS,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(CHURN_PROBABILITY), 1) AS PREDICTED_PCT, ROUND(100 * AVG(CHURNED_NEXT_3M), 1) AS ACTUAL_PCT
FROM s GROUP BY 2
UNION ALL
SELECT 'SEGMENT', SEGMENT, COUNT(*), ROUND(100 * AVG(CHURN_PROBABILITY), 1), ROUND(100 * AVG(CHURNED_NEXT_3M), 1)
FROM s GROUP BY 2;
SELECT * FROM MODEL_VALIDATION ORDER BY CUT, PREDICTED_PCT DESC;

-- 3. Champion vs challenger: every run in the experiment, one row per run
SHOW RUN METRICS IN EXPERIMENT RB_ATTRITION;
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE MODEL_CHALLENGERS AS
SELECT "run_name" AS RUN_NAME,
       MAX(IFF("name" = 'auc', "value", NULL)) AS AUC,
       MAX(IFF("name" = 'avg_precision', "value", NULL)) AS AVG_PRECISION,
       MAX(IFF("name" = 'lift_top_decile', "value", NULL)) AS LIFT_TOP_DECILE,
       MAX(IFF("name" = 'precision_top_decile', "value", NULL)) AS PRECISION_TOP_DECILE
FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID())) GROUP BY 1;
SELECT c.*, STARTSWITH(i.PURPOSE, SPLIT_PART(c.RUN_NAME, '_1', 1)) AS IS_CHAMPION
FROM MODEL_CHALLENGERS c CROSS JOIN (SELECT PURPOSE FROM MODEL_INVENTORY WHERE IS_DEFAULT) i
ORDER BY AUC DESC;

-- 4. Model card, drafted by AI from the evidence only; a person signs it off
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE MODEL_CARD AS
SELECT i.MODEL_NAME, i.VERSION,
       AI_COMPLETE('claude-sonnet-4-5',
         'Write a model card in plain English, under 200 words, as short labelled lines (no markdown): Purpose, Permitted use, Data, '
         || 'Performance, Champion vs challenger, Known limitations, Conditions for use. Only state what these facts support. '
         || 'Model ' || i.MODEL_NAME || ' ' || i.VERSION || ' (' || COALESCE(i.FRAMEWORK, 'scikit-learn') || '), AUC ' || ROUND(i.AUC, 3)
         || '. Purpose: ' || i.PURPOSE || '. Permitted use: ' || i.PERMITTED_USE || '. Data: ' || i.TRAINING_DATA
         || '. Predicted vs actual leave rate (%) by group: ' || v.SUMMARY || '. Experiment runs: ' || c.SUMMARY || '.') AS CARD,
       CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() AS DRAFTED_AT
FROM MODEL_INVENTORY i
CROSS JOIN (SELECT LISTAGG(CUT || ' ' || GROUP_NAME || ' ' || PREDICTED_PCT || ' vs ' || ACTUAL_PCT, '; ') AS SUMMARY FROM MODEL_VALIDATION) v
CROSS JOIN (SELECT LISTAGG(RUN_NAME || ' AUC ' || AUC || ' lift ' || LIFT_TOP_DECILE, '; ') AS SUMMARY FROM MODEL_CHALLENGERS) c
WHERE i.IS_DEFAULT;
SELECT CARD FROM MODEL_CARD;

-- 5. Approval: who decided what, with conditions; the inventory status follows the decision
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE MODEL_APPROVALS (
    MODEL_NAME VARCHAR, VERSION VARCHAR, DECISION VARCHAR, CONDITIONS VARCHAR, APPROVER VARCHAR, DECIDED_AT TIMESTAMP_LTZ
);
INSERT INTO MODEL_APPROVALS
SELECT MODEL_NAME, VERSION, 'APPROVED_WITH_CONDITIONS',
       'Use for ranking only: probabilities run high against actual outcomes, so recalibrate before quoting them. Review quarterly.',
       CURRENT_USER(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
FROM MODEL_INVENTORY WHERE IS_DEFAULT;
UPDATE MODEL_INVENTORY i SET STATUS = a.DECISION FROM MODEL_APPROVALS a WHERE a.MODEL_NAME = i.MODEL_NAME AND a.VERSION = i.VERSION;
SELECT i.MODEL_NAME, i.VERSION, i.STATUS, a.CONDITIONS, a.APPROVER, a.DECIDED_AT
FROM MODEL_INVENTORY i JOIN MODEL_APPROVALS a USING (MODEL_NAME, VERSION);

modules.title: Calibrate the attrition model and predict customer margin
modules.prerequisites: DS1, or `setup/catchup/ds1_model.sql` (uses `ML.RB_CHURN_FEATURES` and the `RB_ATTRITION` experiment)
modules.question: The retention team wants to put a value on every customer at risk. Are DS1's churn scores real probabilities they can multiply by money, and how much will each customer actually be worth over the next few months?
build: Two new runs in experiment `ML.RB_ATTRITION`, comparing DS1's class-weighted XGBoost with an isotonic-calibrated one on AUC, Brier score and calibration error
A calibrated version of `ML.RB_ATTRITION_MODEL` in the Model Registry, registered as a challenger (not the default)
Experiment `ML.RB_MARGIN`: a "margin stays flat" baseline against Ridge and XGBoost models of next-3-month margin
Model `ML.RB_MARGIN_MODEL` in the Model Registry
Table `ML.RB_CUSTOMER_PREDICTIONS`: every customer's calibrated chance of leaving and predicted monthly margin, which DA5 turns into lifetime value and value at risk

steps.title: Open the starter notebook
steps.body:
1. Open `notebooks/` > **ds4_customer_value.ipynb**.
2. Connect it to the notebook service you made in DS1 (the arrow next to the status dot > **Select service**, usually `USER_SERVICE_1`). No service yet? Create one as in DS1: **NOTEBOOK_POOL**, **1 hour**, **HOL_NOTEBOOK_ACCESS_INTEGRATION** (leave it empty on a trial account).
3. Check the role is **HOL_PARTICIPANT** and the warehouse is **BANKING_WH**.
4. Open the **Cortex Code** sidebar (round button, bottom right). You'll paste each step's prompt there.
steps.expect: the starter notebook open with four numbered headings

steps.title: Are the scores probabilities?
steps.body: A score can rank customers well and still not be a probability. DS1 trained XGBoost with `scale_pos_weight` to handle the imbalance, which pushes its scores up.
steps.where: the Cortex Code sidebar, with `ds4_customer_value` open
steps.prompt: In the open notebook ds4_customer_value, put each cell I ask for under its matching numbered heading. Under heading 1, add a SQL cell named score_check that joins BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_ATTRITION_SCORES to RB_CHURN_FEATURES and shows, for each of 10 score deciles, the customer count, the average CHURN_PROBABILITY and the share who actually left (CHURNED_NEXT_3M). Then add a Python cell named reliability that draws the same as a reliability chart: average score against actual leave rate per decile, with the diagonal for a perfectly calibrated model. Run both.
steps.expect: the points sit far above the diagonal. The top decile's average score is far higher than the share who really left (2% leave overall). The model ranks well; its numbers just aren't probabilities.

steps.title: Calibrate, and track it
steps.body:
**Tip:** a calibrator wraps the pipeline, which hides XGBoost from the registry's dependency detection. Naming `conda_dependencies` avoids a "No module named xgboost" error when it registers.
Then compare the runs: **AI & ML > Experiments** > **RB_ATTRITION**, tick the two new runs, **Compare**.
steps.prompt: Under heading 2, add a Python cell named calibrate that sets the session's database and schema to BANKING_HOL.ML and runs the training as a Snowflake ML Job with the @remote decorator from snowflake.ml.jobs (compute pool DS_TRAINING_POOL, stage BANKING_HOL.ML.JOB_STAGE). Inside the job: read RB_CHURN_FEATURES into pandas, split 70/30 stratified (random_state 42), and train two scikit-learn pipelines on the same features as DS1: XGBoost with scale_pos_weight (DS1's approach) and XGBoost without it wrapped in CalibratedClassifierCV with method isotonic and cv 3. Track each as a run in the experiment RB_ATTRITION with snowflake.ml.experiment.ExperimentTracking, with timestamped run names, logging AUC, Brier score, calibration error (the size-weighted average gap between predicted and actual leave rate across 10 score deciles), mean predicted and actual leave rate. Log the calibrated model to the Model Registry as a new version of RB_ATTRITION_MODEL with conda_dependencies scikit-learn and xgboost, target platform WAREHOUSE and a comment saying it is a calibrated challenger, and do not make it the default. Return the metrics, submit the job, wait and print the result. Run it.
steps.expect: similar AUC (the ranking barely changes), but the calibrated run's Brier score and calibration error are far lower, and its mean predicted leave rate matches the actual rate of about 2%

steps.title: Predict margin, against a baseline
steps.body: Lifetime value needs a margin per customer. The simplest assumption is that next month looks like the last 12: that's the baseline any model has to beat.
steps.prompt: Under heading 3, add a Python cell named margin that runs as an ML Job the same way. Inside the job: build a training set from RB_CHURN_FEATURES plus, from BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.RB_MONTHLY_SNAPSHOT up to 31 Aug 2026, each customer's average monthly PROFIT_GBP over the last 3 and last 12 months and average REVENUE_GBP and COST_TO_SERVE_GBP over the last 3 months. The target MARGIN_NEXT_3M is their average monthly PROFIT_GBP in the 3 months after 31 Aug 2026, excluding churned months; train only on customers who have it. Split 70/30 (random_state 42). In a new experiment RB_MARGIN, log a run for the flat baseline (the last-12-month average as the prediction), then Ridge and XGBoost regressors (reg:absoluteerror) as scikit-learn pipelines, each with mean absolute error, MAE against the baseline in percent and total error in percent. Register the model with the lowest MAE as RB_MARGIN_MODEL (conda_dependencies scikit-learn and xgboost, target platform WAREHOUSE, a comment naming the experiment), make it the default, and return the metrics. Run it.
steps.expect: the flat baseline is hard to beat. A simple linear model edges it (a few percent lower error); XGBoost may do worse. Register the one that wins, not the one that sounds cleverest.

steps.title: Score every customer with both models
steps.prompt: Under heading 4, add a Python cell named predictions that scores every customer in RB_CHURN_FEATURES with the calibrated version of RB_ATTRITION_MODEL (predict_proba) and the default version of RB_MARGIN_MODEL (predict, on the same inputs as training), and writes CUSTOMER_ID, CHURN_3M, PREDICTED_MONTHLY_MARGIN_GBP and both model version names to BANKING_HOL.ML.RB_CUSTOMER_PREDICTIONS. Then add a SQL cell named prediction_summary showing the customer count, average CHURN_3M against the actual leave rate, and total predicted monthly margin. Run both.
steps.expect: about 18,400 customers, an average chance of leaving of about 2% (matching what really happened), and about £20 of predicted margin per customer a month

modules.check: - Experiment `RB_ATTRITION` has the calibrated run, and `RB_ATTRITION_MODEL` has a calibrated version that isn't the default - Experiment `RB_MARGIN` has a baseline and at least one model, and `RB_MARGIN_MODEL` is registered - `RB_CUSTOMER_PREDICTIONS` has a calibrated chance of leaving and a predicted margin for every customer
modules.note: - **Calibrate before anyone multiplies.** Pricing, provisions, lifetime value and campaign budgets all treat model outputs as probabilities. A model trained with class weights or resampling needs calibrating first, and calibration error belongs in its validation pack alongside AUC. - **Champion and challenger.** The calibrated model is a new version, not a replacement: DS3's model risk process decides whether it becomes the default. - **Always log the baseline.** "Margin stays flat" is a model too. Recording it in the experiment is what shows a reviewer the new model earns its complexity. - **Hand over a table, not a notebook.** `RB_CUSTOMER_PREDICTIONS` records which model versions produced each number, so DA5's lifetime value and every campaign built on it trace back to the registry.

modules.title: Corporate Payments 360 agent
modules.prerequisites: DA2 (`SV_CLIENT_360`), or run `client_360.sql` if you skipped it
modules.question: Before I call a client, tell me everything: payments health, open incidents and what they have been complaining about.
build: Agent `SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE.AGENTS.CORPORATE_PAYMENTS_360` with an Analyst tool on your `SV_CLIENT_360` and charting

steps.title: Create the agent with Cortex Code
steps.body:
1. Rename the new agent file to `corporate_payments_360` straight away. It opens as "Untitled".

Cortex Code then guides you through the configuration.
steps.prompt: Create a Cortex Agent SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE.AGENTS.CORPORATE_PAYMENTS_360 with display name "Corporate Payments 360". It supports Payments Operations and Relationship Managers in a UK corporate bank. Tools: a Cortex Analyst tool Client360 on semantic view BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.SV_CLIENT_360 (client health, alerts, sentiment) on warehouse BANKING_WH, plus charting. Response instructions: lead with a one-line summary, format money in GBP with thousands separators and percentages to 1 dp, and when briefing on a client always cover payment volume and success rate, failed value, open and critical alerts, and feedback sentiment with the main topic. steps.mediaCaption: + Add new > Agent > name it corporate_payments_360 > Create with CoCo > paste the brief

steps.title: Ask it in Snowflake CoWork
steps.body:
1. Run the four sample questions.
2. Start with "Brief me on the client with the most failed payment value".
steps.where: Snowsight > **AI & ML > CoWork** (formerly Snowflake Intelligence) > **Corporate Payments 360**
steps.expect: a briefing naming the client, failed value, open and critical alerts, and the main feedback topic. The sector question returns a chart.
steps.mediaCaption: Snowflake CoWork > pick Corporate Payments 360 > ask the first question

steps.title: See how it answered

1. Expand **Show details** on an answer.
It shows which tool the agent chose and the SQL that ran.
steps.expect: each answer used `Client360`, with the SQL it generated over `SV_CLIENT_360`

steps.title: Improve it
steps.where: the Cortex Code sidebar, with `corporate_payments_360` open
steps.prompt: Add a sample question to CORPORATE_PAYMENTS_360 for "Which of Priya Sharma's clients have open critical alerts?" and update its orchestration instructions so questions about a named RM always filter on RM name. Redeploy it.

-- =====================================================
-- VIGNETTE OPS1: CORPORATE PAYMENTS 360 AGENT   (~45 min)
-- Persona: Payments Operations analyst (no SQL needed after setup)
-- Question: "Before I call a client, tell me everything: payments health,
--            open incidents, and what they have been complaining about."
-- Prereq:   DA2 (SV_CLIENT_360), or setup/catchup/client_360.sql if you skipped it
-- =====================================================

USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;   -- see exactly what an attendee sees
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- OPS1.1 The agent: the DA2 semantic view as a tool + charting
-- Created in SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE.AGENTS so it appears in Snowflake CoWork
-- for everyone with access.
-- (Snowsight alternative: AI & ML > Agents > Create agent - same settings.)
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE.AGENTS.CORPORATE_PAYMENTS_360
  COMMENT = 'Banking HOL - Corporate Payments 360: client payments health, incidents and sentiment'
  PROFILE = '{"display_name": "Corporate Payments 360", "color": "blue"}'
  FROM SPECIFICATION
  $$
  models:
    orchestration: auto

  orchestration:
    budget:
      seconds: 90
      tokens: 20000

  instructions:
    response: >
      You support Payments Operations and Relationship Managers in a UK corporate bank.
      Lead with a one-line summary, then the supporting numbers.
      Format money in GBP with thousands separators and percentages to 1 decimal place.
      When briefing on a client, always cover: payment volume and success rate,
      failed value, open and critical alerts, and feedback sentiment with the main topic.
      If the data cannot answer the question, say so - never guess.
    orchestration: >
      Use Client360 for questions about clients, relationship managers,
      KYC status, payment totals and success rates, alerts or incidents, and client feedback.
      For a client briefing you may need Client360 more than once.
    sample_questions:
      - question: "Brief me on the client with the most failed payment value"
      - question: "Which relationship managers have the most open critical alerts?"
      - question: "Which clients have negative sentiment and a success rate below 96%?"
      - question: "Show failed payment value by sector as a chart"

  tools:
    - tool_spec:
        type: cortex_analyst_text_to_sql
        name: Client360
        description: >
          Corporate client 360: one row per client with sector, country, KYC status and RM;
          payment totals, success rate and failed value per client; AI-scored feedback
          sentiment and topic; and operational alerts with severity, status and resolution time.
    - tool_spec:
        type: data_to_chart
        name: data_to_chart
        description: Generates charts from query results

  tool_resources:
    Client360:
      semantic_view: BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS.SV_CLIENT_360
      execution_environment:
        type: warehouse
        warehouse: BANKING_WH
  $$;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- OPS1.2 Use it - Snowflake CoWork (formerly Snowflake Intelligence)
-- Select "Corporate Payments 360" and try:
--   1. "Brief me on the client with the most failed payment value"
--   2. "Which of Priya Sharma's clients have open critical alerts?"
--   3. "Show failed payment value by sector as a chart"
--   4. "Which clients have negative sentiment AND a success rate below 96%?"
-- Expand "Show details" on each answer to see the tool and SQL used.
-- -----------------------------------------------------

-- OPS1.3 The same agent from SQL (e.g. embedding in a process or app)
SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.DATA_AGENT_RUN(
  'SNOWFLAKE_INTELLIGENCE.AGENTS.CORPORATE_PAYMENTS_360',
  $${"messages":[{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Which relationship managers have the most open critical alerts?"}]}]}$$
) AS RESPONSE;

-- In your bank: agents inherit the caller's role - an RM only ever
-- sees what their role is granted (see GOV1 for masking and row access).

SELECT 'OPS1 complete' AS STATUS;

modules.sql:
-- =====================================================
-- VIGNETTE OPS2: ALERT TRIAGE + NEGATIVE SENTIMENT FEED   (~30 min)
-- Persona: Payments Operations analyst / team lead
-- Question: "Which open alerts should my team work first, what should we do,
--            and which unhappy clients are linked to them?"
-- Prereq:   setup/catchup/core_analytics.sql (FEEDBACK_ENRICHED, STG_* views)
-- =====================================================

USE ROLE HOL_PARTICIPANT;
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;   -- see exactly what an attendee sees
USE WAREHOUSE BANKING_WH;
USE SCHEMA BANKING_HOL.ANALYTICS;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- OPS2.1 Live negative-sentiment feed for the CX escalation queue
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE DT_NEGATIVE_SENTIMENT_FEED
    TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'
    WAREHOUSE  = BANKING_WH
AS
SELECT FEEDBACK_ID, FEEDBACK_DATE, CUSTOMER_ID, CUSTOMER_NAME, CUSTOMER_SECTOR,
       RM_NAME, PAYMENT_ID, PAYMENT_TYPE, FEEDBACK_TEXT, SENTIMENT_SCORE, TOPIC_CATEGORY
FROM FEEDBACK_ENRICHED
WHERE SENTIMENT_LABEL = 'NEGATIVE';

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- OPS2.2 Prioritised triage queue: open alerts, scored for urgency
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW V_ALERT_TRIAGE_QUEUE AS
SELECT al.ALERT_ID, al.ALERT_TIME, al.SEVERITY, al.STATUS, al.ASSIGNED_TO,
       al.PAYMENT_TYPE, al.ALERT_DESCRIPTION,
       p.PAYMENT_ID, p.AMOUNT, p.CURRENCY, p.STATUS AS PAYMENT_STATUS,
       e.ERROR_CODE, e.ERROR_DESCRIPTION, e.ERROR_CATEGORY, e.IS_RETRYABLE,
       c.CUSTOMER_NAME, c.RM_NAME,
       COUNT(n.FEEDBACK_ID) AS CLIENT_NEGATIVE_FEEDBACK,
       -- simple, explainable priority score
       DECODE(al.SEVERITY, 'CRITICAL', 40, 'HIGH', 25, 'MEDIUM', 10, 0)
         + IFF(p.AMOUNT >= 1000000, 30, IFF(p.AMOUNT >= 100000, 15, 0))
         + LEAST(COUNT(n.FEEDBACK_ID), 20)
         + IFF(e.ERROR_CATEGORY = 'COMPLIANCE', 10, 0)        AS PRIORITY_SCORE
FROM BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.OPERATIONAL_ALERTS al
JOIN STG_PAYMENTS p          ON al.PAYMENT_ID = p.PAYMENT_ID
LEFT JOIN BANKING_HOL.RAW_DATA.ERROR_CODES e ON p.ERROR_CODE = e.ERROR_CODE
LEFT JOIN STG_ACCOUNTS a     ON p.ORIGINATOR_ACCOUNT_ID = a.ACCOUNT_ID
LEFT JOIN STG_CUSTOMERS c    ON a.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
LEFT JOIN DT_NEGATIVE_SENTIMENT_FEED n ON n.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
WHERE al.STATUS <> 'RESOLVED'
GROUP BY ALL;

SELECT ALERT_ID, SEVERITY, PAYMENT_TYPE, AMOUNT, ERROR_DESCRIPTION, CUSTOMER_NAME,
       CLIENT_NEGATIVE_FEEDBACK, PRIORITY_SCORE
FROM V_ALERT_TRIAGE_QUEUE
ORDER BY PRIORITY_SCORE DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- OPS2.3 AI-recommended next action for the top of the queue
-- -----------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ALERT_RECOMMENDATIONS AS
SELECT ALERT_ID, SEVERITY, PAYMENT_TYPE, CUSTOMER_NAME, RM_NAME, PRIORITY_SCORE,
       AI_COMPLETE('claude-sonnet-4-5',
         'You are a senior payments operations analyst at a UK bank. In at most 3 short bullet points, '
         || 'give the next actions for this alert, including whether to retry the payment and whether to contact the client or their RM. '
         || 'Alert: ' || ALERT_DESCRIPTION
         || ' | Scheme: ' || PAYMENT_TYPE
         || ' | Error: ' || COALESCE(ERROR_DESCRIPTION, 'none') || ' (' || COALESCE(ERROR_CATEGORY, 'n/a')
         || ', retryable=' || COALESCE(IS_RETRYABLE::STRING, 'unknown') || ')'
         || ' | Amount: ' || AMOUNT || ' ' || CURRENCY
         || ' | Client negative feedback items: ' || CLIENT_NEGATIVE_FEEDBACK) AS RECOMMENDED_ACTION
FROM V_ALERT_TRIAGE_QUEUE
ORDER BY PRIORITY_SCORE DESC
LIMIT 10;

SELECT ALERT_ID, SEVERITY, CUSTOMER_NAME, RECOMMENDED_ACTION
FROM ALERT_RECOMMENDATIONS ORDER BY PRIORITY_SCORE DESC;

-- -----------------------------------------------------
-- OPS2.4 Hand it to the business
--  * Add V_ALERT_TRIAGE_QUEUE to SV_CLIENT_360 (ask CoCo to extend DA2's view), or
--  * Open payments-dashboard/ (Streamlit) and ask CoCo:
--    "Add a 'Triage' page to the Streamlit app that shows V_ALERT_TRIAGE_QUEUE
--     ordered by PRIORITY_SCORE with ALERT_RECOMMENDATIONS alongside."
-- -----------------------------------------------------

SELECT 'OPS2 complete' AS STATUS;

modules.persona: Payments Ops lead / relationship manager (business user)

modules.question: I run payments operations, not SQL. Can I ask about failures in plain English, get a chart I can keep, investigate why a sector is getting worse, have the weekly numbers sent to me automatically, hand a relationship manager a briefing deck, and publish a dashboard my team opens every morning?

A **Deep Research** report on why a sector's payment failures are rising

steps.title: Open CoWork with the payments agent
steps.body:
CoWork opens on its own page.
1. Pick **Payments Ops CoWork** in the agent picker.
2. Open the settings under your name.
3. Check the role is **HOL_PARTICIPANT** and the warehouse is **BANKING_WH**.
steps.where: Snowsight > **AI & ML > CoWork** (or the CoWork app), then choose the agent **Payments Ops CoWork**
steps.prompt: What can you tell me about our payments? Give me a short overview of volume, failures and the clients and schemes that matter most this year.
steps.expect: a plain-English overview with a few numbers and a table or chart. Open **Show details** under the answer to see the SQL the agent generated and the semantic view it used: every answer is traceable.
steps.pasteInto: the **CoWork** chat box (not the Cortex Code sidebar)
steps.mediaCaption: Snowflake CoWork > pick Payments Ops CoWork > paste the overview prompt

steps.title: Make a chart and save it
steps.prompt: Show monthly failed payment value by scheme for the last 12 months as a stacked bar chart, with SEPA in red.
steps.expect: a stacked bar chart, with a note on how it was built. Use the chart's **Save** option to keep it as a **chart artifact**: it re-runs its query when you open it, with your own access, so it stays current. Then use **Share** on the conversation to save it as a **thread** snapshot. Find both under **Projects > Artifacts**.

steps.title: Investigate with Deep Research
steps.prompt: What are Logistics clients saying in their feedback over the last four months compared with the rest of the year, are any of them talking about leaving us, do their payment failures explain it, and what should their relationship managers do first?
steps.expect: CoWork splits the question into several investigations, runs them in parallel and writes a structured report in up to 10 minutes, with every claim traced to its query. Logistics feedback has turned negative recently, and Logistics clients are the only ones talking about reviewing other banks, moving their payments or tendering their banking (the same story DA1 finds). Their payment failure rate isn't unusually high, so the report should point at service and communication rather than payment failures: that's the kind of conclusion a single chart wouldn't give you. Ask a follow-up such as "break that down by relationship manager": it runs as a normal chat turn on top of the report.
